section: 3. Time and Frequency Are Complementary Views
claim: A waveform makes temporal structure visible but hides much of the organization of frequency.

section: 3. Time and Frequency Are Complementary Views
claim: A long-term spectrum summarizes frequency content but destroys the sequence of events.

section: 3. Time and Frequency Are Complementary Views
claim: The short-time Fourier transform (STFT) is therefore one of the foundational tools of computational hearing because it trades absolute temporal precision for localized frequency information [6].

section: 3. Time and Frequency Are Complementary Views
claim: For a discrete signal x[n] and analysis window w[n], the STFT evaluates local spectral content around successive time positions.

section: 3. Time and Frequency Are Complementary Views

section: 3. Time and Frequency Are Complementary Views

section: 3. Time and Frequency Are Complementary Views

section: 3. Time and Frequency Are Complementary Views

section: 3. Time and Frequency Are Complementary Views

section: 3. Time and Frequency Are Complementary Views

section: 3. Time and Frequency Are Complementary Views

section: 4. Frequency Selectivity and the Idea of an Auditory Filterbank
claim: Human hearing does not analyze frequency with uniformly spaced Fourier bins.

section: 4. Frequency Selectivity and the Idea of an Auditory Filterbank
claim: The cochlear partition behaves approximately like a bank of overlapping band-pass filters whose bandwidth increases with center frequency.

section: 4. Frequency Selectivity and the Idea of an Auditory Filterbank
claim: Psychoacoustic research has described these frequency-selective channels using critical bands, equivalent rectangular bandwidth (ERB), and related models [2,7,8].

section: 4. Frequency Selectivity and the Idea of an Auditory Filterbank
claim: One widely used approximation by Glasberg and Moore expresses the ERB in hertz as a function of center frequency f.

section: 4. Frequency Selectivity and the Idea of an Auditory Filterbank
claim: It captures the fact that auditory filters become broader at higher frequencies [7].

section: 4. Frequency Selectivity and the Idea of an Auditory Filterbank

section: 4. Frequency Selectivity and the Idea of an Auditory Filterbank

section: 4. Frequency Selectivity and the Idea of an Auditory Filterbank
claim: The technical question is whether the transform exposes structure useful for AI-music judgment.

section: 4. Frequency Selectivity and the Idea of an Auditory Filterbank
claim: Human-inspired channels may be valuable because many production phenomena are perceptually meaningful only relative to auditory bandwidth, masking, or frequency-dependent resolution.

section: 4. Frequency Selectivity and the Idea of an Auditory Filterbank
claim: But they should coexist with conventional spectral features and learned front ends rather than replace them by ideology.

section: 4. Frequency Selectivity and the Idea of an Auditory Filterbank
claim: The Ear v1 sensor layer can therefore maintain parallel views: linear-frequency STFT measurements for engineering precision, perceptually warped or auditory-filterbank views for perceptual organization, and learned representations for patterns that are not easily specified in advance.

section: 5. The Mel Scale Is Useful, but It Is Not the Ear

section: 5. The Mel Scale Is Useful, but It Is Not the Ear

section: 5. The Mel Scale Is Useful, but It Is Not the Ear

section: 5. The Mel Scale Is Useful, but It Is Not the Ear

section: 5. The Mel Scale Is Useful, but It Is Not the Ear

section: 6. Hearing Happens at Multiple Time Scales

section: 6. Hearing Happens at Multiple Time Scales

section: 6. Hearing Happens at Multiple Time Scales

section: 6. Hearing Happens at Multiple Time Scales

section: 7. Level, Loudness and the Difference Between Energy and Perception
claim: Signal amplitude and perceived loudness are related but not identical.

section: 7. Level, Loudness and the Difference Between Energy and Perception
claim: Human sensitivity varies strongly with frequency and level, and loudness perception involves frequency weighting and temporal integration.

section: 7. Level, Loudness and the Difference Between Energy and Perception
claim: Psychoacoustic work by Zwicker, Fastl, Moore and others provides detailed models of these relationships [2,8,12].

section: 7. Level, Loudness and the Difference Between Energy and Perception
claim: Broadcast and production standards such as ITU-R BS.1770 translate part of this knowledge into practical loudness measurement using frequency weighting and gated integration [13].

section: 7. Level, Loudness and the Difference Between Energy and Perception
claim: Moodify must keep three layers distinct. *Physical level* concerns sample amplitude and power. *Standardized loudness measurement* concerns metrics such as LUFS under a defined algorithm. *Auditory judgment* concerns what that loudness means in context.

section: 7. Level, Loudness and the Difference Between Energy and Perception
claim: Confusing these layers produces false certainty.

section: 7. Level, Loudness and the Difference Between Energy and Perception
claim: For example, integrated loudness can be measured very reliably, yet the conclusion “too loud” cannot be universal.

section: 7. Level, Loudness and the Difference Between Energy and Perception
claim: It depends on platform, genre, artistic intent, crest factor, dynamic behavior, reference population and downstream normalization.

section: 7. Level, Loudness and the Difference Between Energy and Perception
claim: The Ear should store the measurement as fact, contextualize it, and only then generate a judgment with stated assumptions.

section: 7. Level, Loudness and the Difference Between Energy and Perception
claim: This pattern recurs throughout machine hearing: the closer a metric is to physics, the easier it is to reproduce; the closer a claim is to meaning, the more context and uncertainty must be modeled.
Stereo audio gives the Ear access to relationships that do not exist in a single monophonic waveform.
Inter-channel level differences, timing differences, phase relationships, correlation and frequency-dependent spatial behavior all contribute to perceived width and localization [14].
A simple normalized correlation coefficient between left and right channels can summarize one aspect of similarity, but it should not be interpreted as a complete spatial diagnosis.
A wide, decorrelated ambience may be artistically appropriate; sustained negative correlation in low-frequency content may create mono-compatibility risk.
The same global statistic can hide both situations.
Moodify should therefore treat spatial hearing as a time-frequency problem.
Global correlation can be retained as a summary, while localized inter-channel energy, phase and coherence measurements provide evidence for specific findings.
Spatial judgments should also be frequency-aware, because phase behavior at 80 Hz and 8 kHz has different perceptual and technical consequences.

This is an example of why the Ear needs interpretation rather than thresholds alone. “Correlation below zero” is not automatically “bad.” The system must ask where, for how long, in what frequency region, and with what likely consequence.

section: 9. Masking and the Limits of Visible Energy
claim: Two sounds can both be physically present while one becomes perceptually difficult to hear.

section: 9. Masking and the Limits of Visible Energy

section: 9. Masking and the Limits of Visible Energy
claim: For Moodify, masking is important because a spectral plot that shows energy in two sources or regions does not tell us whether one perceptually obscures another.

section: 9. Masking and the Limits of Visible Energy
claim: In a final stereo mix, source separation may be imperfect or unavailable, so masking inference must often remain probabilistic.

section: 9. Masking and the Limits of Visible Energy
claim: Nevertheless, local spectral overlap, level relationships, modulation patterns and learned source-aware features can provide evidence.

section: 9. Masking and the Limits of Visible Energy
claim: A future vocal-masking judgment, for example, should not be emitted merely because there is energy in the same frequency band as the voice.

section: 9. Masking and the Limits of Visible Energy
claim: The Ear should combine source or vocal likelihood, local spectral competition, relative level, temporal coincidence and confidence in the separation or embedding used.

section: 9. Masking and the Limits of Visible Energy

section: 9. Masking and the Limits of Visible Energy

section: 10. Auditory Scene Analysis: Hearing Objects in a Mixture
claim: Bregman’s theory of auditory scene analysis frames hearing as the organization of acoustic mixtures into perceptual streams and events [4].

section: 10. Auditory Scene Analysis: Hearing Objects in a Mixture
claim: The listener does not normally experience a song as a single pressure curve.

section: 10. Auditory Scene Analysis: Hearing Objects in a Mixture
claim: Voices, instruments, reverberant spaces, rhythmic events and background textures emerge as partially coherent auditory objects.

section: 10. Auditory Scene Analysis: Hearing Objects in a Mixture
claim: A machine-hearing system can approach this organization through source separation, event detection, embedding similarity, onset grouping, harmonicity, spatial cues, repetition and learned attention.

section: 10. Auditory Scene Analysis: Hearing Objects in a Mixture
claim: More importantly, Moodify Ear v1 does not need perfect source separation before it can be useful.

section: 10. Auditory Scene Analysis: Hearing Objects in a Mixture

section: 10. Auditory Scene Analysis: Hearing Objects in a Mixture
claim: The representation can therefore contain *soft auditory objects*: regions or streams represented with probabilities rather than absolute identities.

section: 10. Auditory Scene Analysis: Hearing Objects in a Mixture
claim: A segment may be 0.86 likely to contain lead vocal energy and 0.44 likely to contain bright synthetic texture.

section: 10. Auditory Scene Analysis: Hearing Objects in a Mixture
claim: A judgment can use these probabilities and carry their uncertainty forward.

section: 10. Auditory Scene Analysis: Hearing Objects in a Mixture
claim: This avoids a brittle architecture in which every higher-level finding depends on a perfect transcription of the scene.

section: 10. Auditory Scene Analysis: Hearing Objects in a Mixture

Frequency energy alone does not explain why a listener hears a stable pitch, a harmonic source, or a note that persists through changing timbre.
Pitch perception depends on periodicity, harmonic relations, resolved and unresolved components, temporal cues and context.
Computational estimators such as YIN demonstrate that even apparently simple fundamental-frequency tracking requires explicit treatment of ambiguity and error [23].
For Moodify, pitch and harmonicity are valuable less as ends in themselves than as organizing cues.
Stable harmonic stacks can help distinguish pitched components from noise-like texture.
Sudden changes in harmonic consistency may indicate source transitions, synthesis instability or intentionally inharmonic material.
Tonal estimates can also help align WSE evidence with MSE structure.
The Ear should therefore avoid treating “pitch detected” as a binary fact.
A useful pitch state contains candidate frequencies, confidence, voicing or periodicity evidence, local harmonic consistency and time continuity.
In polyphonic music, multiple concurrent pitch structures may exist, and a single F0 estimate may be actively misleading.
This again supports soft auditory objects rather than brittle labels.
A region can carry a probability of harmonic organization without forcing Moodify to claim that it has perfectly transcribed the underlying notes.

section: 11. Invariance and Sensitivity: What Should the Ear Ignore?
claim: An intelligent representation must be stable to changes that do not alter the phenomenon of interest and sensitive to changes that do.

section: 11. Invariance and Sensitivity: What Should the Ear Ignore?
claim: If a harmless metadata rewrite changes the Ear’s judgment, the representation is unstable.

section: 11. Invariance and Sensitivity: What Should the Ear Ignore?
claim: If a severe phase cancellation leaves the representation unchanged, it is insensitive.

section: 11. Invariance and Sensitivity: What Should the Ear Ignore?
claim: Let T_n denote a nuisance transformation that should not materially affect a judgment, and T_s a signal transformation that should.

section: 11. Invariance and Sensitivity: What Should the Ear Ignore?
claim: For an appropriate representation distance d, a useful system seeks small change under T_n and sufficiently large change under T_s.

section: 11. Invariance and Sensitivity: What Should the Ear Ignore?
claim: The meaning of “nuisance” depends on the task.

section: 11. Invariance and Sensitivity: What Should the Ear Ignore?
claim: Global gain may be irrelevant to timbre classification but essential to clipping or loudness analysis.

section: 11. Invariance and Sensitivity: What Should the Ear Ignore?

section: 11. Invariance and Sensitivity: What Should the Ear Ignore?
claim: Therefore invariance should be defined per judgment family rather than baked into one universal embedding.

claim: Different subspaces can preserve different sensitivities while a higher layer decides which evidence is relevant to the current question.

Classical audio analysis relies on explicit descriptors: RMS energy, spectral centroid, rolloff, zero-crossing rate, crest factor, phase correlation, modulation, onset strength, chroma and many others.
These features are interpretable and often deterministic.
Their weakness is that the designer must anticipate what matters.
Modern representation learning shifts part of that burden to data. wav2vec 2.0 demonstrated strong self-supervised representation learning for speech [16].
LEAF showed that an audio front end itself can be learned rather than fixed [17].
PANNs and Audio Spectrogram Transformer demonstrated transferable representations from large-scale audio classification [18,19].
BEATs extended self-supervised audio pretraining using iterative acoustic tokenizers [20].
Audio-MAE used masked spectrogram reconstruction for general audio representation learning [21].
For music, MERT and related work demonstrate the value of domain-specific pretraining and music-aware objectives [22].
Moodify should exploit these advances, but not surrender its architecture to a single opaque embedding.
Learned representations are strongest when paired with explicit evidence channels that retain engineering meaning.

A practical Ear v1 can therefore use a hybrid strategy: deterministic measurements for auditability, human-inspired transforms for perceptual organization, and learned embeddings for pattern discovery and semantic context.

section: 15. AI-Generated Music Creates New Hearing Problems

For Moodify, machine hearing is not a metaphor for “using AI on audio.” It is a layered technical discipline.

Sound must be acquired under known conditions, transformed into multiple physical and perceptual views, organized across time, related to musical structure, interpreted under context, converted into uncertainty-aware judgments, linked to evidence, and preserved as cases from which future versions can learn.
This definition deliberately makes the technical graph narrower.
Post-processing can remain downstream, but it is not required to define the Ear.

The primary research question becomes whether the representation becomes more informative, the judgments more reliable, the uncertainty better calibrated, and the case library more valuable over time.
Moodify Ear v1 therefore begins with an intentionally modest proposition: before a machine can decide what to do to sound, it must establish a disciplined way to hear it.

The next chapter will examine why conventional audio analysis, despite its sophistication, still falls short of this definition of hearing and where the transition from analyzer to auditory intelligence must occur.

Hearing begins when those instruments become context-sensitive, evidence-aware and capable of learning.
Modern audio software can expose an extraordinary quantity of information.
A single file can be transformed into waveforms, spectrograms, loudness curves, phase plots, chromagrams, onset maps, spectral descriptors, embeddings, source estimates and hundreds of statistics.
The abundance of measurement creates a persuasive illusion: if a machine can describe enough properties of a signal, perhaps it already hears.
Moodify Ear begins by rejecting that equivalence.
Analysis is necessary, but analysis is not yet hearing.
An analyzer answers questions that are already encoded in its measurement design.

Hearing must also decide which observations matter, how they relate, what context changes their meaning, which explanations remain plausible, when a conclusion is unsupported, and how later evidence should alter future behavior.
Measurement becomes more valuable when its epistemic role is clear.
A loudness meter is trustworthy precisely because it does not pretend to know artistic intent.
A spectrum is useful because it tells us something specific about energy distribution, not because it claims to understand a mix.
The Moodify Ear must preserve that discipline as it moves from physical observation to higher-level judgment.
The purpose of this chapter is to define the boundary.

The descriptor fallacy appears when a system treats a feature name as though it were the phenomenon itself.

The label “spectral flatness” sounds perceptual, but the computation is a relation between geometric and arithmetic means of spectral magnitudes. “Rolloff” sounds like a diagnosis, but it is normally a percentile-based frequency descriptor. “Dynamic range” can refer to multiple non-equivalent definitions.
Naming a statistic does not solve the interpretation problem.
This becomes dangerous when user interfaces present descriptors with normative colors.
A value is calculated, compared with an undocumented threshold, and rendered green or red.
The interface has converted a measurement into a judgment without exposing the assumptions between them.
Moodify should instead maintain a three-part separation: *descriptor*, *reference model*, and *judgment*.
The reference model says what population, standard, context or hypothesis gives the value meaning.
The judgment says what the system concludes after combining evidence.
This separation allows the same descriptor to support different judgments.
A high crest factor may be desirable evidence of preserved transients in one case and irrelevant in another.
A narrow stereo image may be completely intentional.
A high-frequency cutoff may be expected from the source format, suspicious in a supposedly lossless master, or musically irrelevant in a section dominated by low-frequency instruments.
The Ear is not created by collecting more descriptors.
It is created by constructing disciplined relations between descriptors and claims.
Music-information-retrieval research has long confronted a semantic gap between low-level signal descriptors and the concepts humans use to discuss music.
Physical measurements can be computed directly, while categories such as mood, texture, instrumentation, production quality or style require additional assumptions and learned mappings [20,21].
The gap is especially important for Moodify because the first product domain is not generic tagging.
The Ear must reason about technical and perceptual conditions in a finished mix.

A system may detect energy near 7 kHz, but the meaningful question could be whether that energy is a vocal sibilance problem, a cymbal characteristic, a codec artifact, a synthesis texture, or simply a normal part of the arrangement.
No increase in FFT resolution solves this by itself.
The missing information is relational and contextual.
The system needs temporal structure, source likelihoods, comparison populations, learned priors, musical sections, uncertainty and, in some cases, human authority.
The semantic gap therefore marks the point at which Moodify must stop behaving like a dashboard and begin behaving like a reasoning system grounded in sound.

The boundary does not disappear when a measurement becomes perceptually motivated.
ITU-R BS.1387, commonly associated with perceptual evaluation of audio quality, defines an objective method intended to estimate perceived differences under specified conditions [8].
Such systems are more sophisticated than raw error metrics because they incorporate auditory models and mappings to perceptual judgments.
Yet a perceptual metric is still a model of a task.
It is not a universal substitute for listening.
Many quality metrics require a reference signal, assume particular distortion families, or have been calibrated using specific subjective datasets.
Reviews of objective audio-quality measures show that performance can vary substantially across tasks and distortion types [23].
Moodify therefore needs a hierarchy of validity.
A metric can be valid for detecting a particular class of degradation without being valid for judging the artistic success of a song.
A model can correlate with human quality scores on compression artifacts without being able to diagnose an AI-generation artifact that has no clean reference.
The Ear should ask not only, “What does this metric output?” but also, “For which class of claims has this metric been validated?”

Every judgment contains a reference, even when the software pretends otherwise. “Too loud” means loud relative to something. “Too much low end” means excessive relative to a target, population, balance, source role or perceptual criterion. “Unusual artifact” means unusual relative to a learned expectation.
Reference design is therefore one of Moodify Ear's central research problems.
Absolute clipping is different from genre-relative spectral balance.
Codec degradation can sometimes be evaluated against a source reference, while generated-music anomalies usually cannot.
The Ear v1 should therefore record the reference basis inside each judgment.

A judgment without a reference basis is difficult to audit and impossible to improve systematically, because a reviewer cannot tell whether the disagreement concerns the measurement or the comparison population.
A common first implementation of audio intelligence is a set of thresholds: if metric m exceeds tau, emit warning y.
Thresholds are useful and sometimes entirely appropriate, but they become misleading when they are treated as universal semantics.
The difficulty is that many audio phenomena are continuous, conditional and interacting.

A high-frequency cutoff at 15 kHz may have one meaning for a 44.1 kHz lossless file, another for a compressed distribution copy, and little importance for source material with naturally limited bandwidth.
A momentary short-term loudness peak may be musically desirable even when a simple rule flags it.
Moodify should retain thresholds as transparent components of evidence, not hide them as truth.

A rule can be expressed as “this observation exceeded threshold tau under reference model R, therefore hypothesis H gained support.” That structure is more robust than “red means bad.” As the Ear learns, thresholds can become conditional surfaces rather than single constants.
But the same principle remains: the decision boundary is part of the model and must be versioned.
A learned system may discover that a certain spectral-temporal pattern is strongly associated with low human ratings or with a known class of AI-generated artifacts.
That association can be operationally useful.
It is not automatically a causal explanation.
This distinction matters because Moodify intends to explain its judgments.

An explanation should indicate what kind of knowledge is being offered. “The energy pattern matches cases previously labeled as artifact class A” is an evidential explanation. “The artifact was caused by model architecture B” is a causal claim and requires stronger evidence.
The Ear should therefore maintain hypotheses rather than prematurely collapse them.
If H is a set of possible explanations, the system may estimate a context-conditioned distribution: The report can expose the leading hypothesis while preserving alternatives.
This is especially important in AI-generated music, where the generation chain may be unknown and different systems may create acoustically similar symptoms through different mechanisms.
Explainability becomes more credible when it states the epistemic level of a claim: measured fact, statistical association, interpretation, or causal hypothesis.
Traditional classification assumes that the important classes are known in advance.
An Ear deployed on rapidly changing generative audio faces an open world.
New models, codecs, synthesis methods and failure patterns can produce observations outside the training distribution.
Under distribution shift, predictive accuracy and confidence can degrade, and uncertainty estimates that look reliable on familiar data may become misleading [16].
For Moodify, this means an unknown acoustic pattern should not be forced into the nearest known artifact label simply because the model requires a class.
The judgment vocabulary therefore needs explicit states for novelty and insufficient evidence.
The Ear can say that a region is anomalous relative to its learned representation while declining to name the cause.
Such an output is scientifically more valuable than a confident misclassification because it creates a candidate case for research.
Open-world behavior converts unknowns into assets.
A recurring cluster of unresolved Production Cases may define the next anomaly class or the next sensor required by Ear v2.
A model can achieve high benchmark accuracy for the wrong reason.

In music-information retrieval, Sturm used the metaphor of a “horse” to describe systems whose apparent success may be explained by confounds or unintended cues rather than the musical concept they are claimed to recognize [18].
This warning is directly relevant to Moodify.

An artifact detector might learn platform encoding signatures, sample-rate conventions, dataset loudness, generator-specific metadata leakage or mastering habits instead of the acoustic phenomenon of interest.
A benchmark score would look impressive while the Ear remained brittle.
Controlled Intervention Lab experiments are one defense.
If the same source is modified by a known transformation while nuisance variables are held constant, the system can be tested for causal sensitivity to the intended change.
Cross-generator and cross-codec splits are another defense.
The deeper rule is that benchmark design is part of hearing research.
The question is not merely whether the model predicts labels, but whether it responds to the right acoustic evidence.

Once a system emits judgments, it must communicate confidence responsibly.
Neural-network probabilities are often poorly calibrated: a prediction reported with 0.9 confidence does not automatically mean that predictions of this type are correct 90 percent of the time [19].
A useful calibration target can be stated conceptually as: Calibration must be evaluated on the domain where the Ear is used.

The chapter can be reduced to eight engineering principles. **1.
Measurement is not meaning.** Every descriptor must retain its limited definition. **2.
Standards have scope.** Operational targets must not be converted into universal aesthetic laws. **3.
Context is part of judgment.** The same observation can mean different things in different musical states. **4.
Every judgment has a reference.** The reference basis must be explicit and versioned. **5.
Correlation is not cause.** The report should distinguish association, interpretation and causal hypothesis. **6.
Unknown is a valid state.** Distribution shift and novel artifacts require abstention. **7.
Evidence precedes authority.** A claim earns trust by being reconstructable, not by being displayed confidently. **8.
Learning happens through cases.** Human review and versioned updates turn analysis into an evolving Ear.
With these principles, the boundary becomes clear.
Audio analysis gives Moodify its instruments.
Hearing begins when those instruments are organized into an evidence-aware, context-sensitive and learning system.

The canonical Ear v1 runtime begins with an immutable audio source and ends with a learning-ready Production Case.
It must be possible to complete the entire path without modifying the source audio.
This pipeline is not a strict claim that every internal computation must execute sequentially.
Sensors may run in parallel, representations may be cached, and multiple judgment heads may consume the same state.
The sequence instead defines authority: later layers may depend on earlier layers, but earlier layers should not silently depend on a downstream product action.
The most important negative requirement is that post-processing is not part of the canonical path.
Processing may exist in the Intervention Lab, but analysis must not require transformation.
Before the Ear listens, it must know what object it is listening to.
The source layer therefore establishes stable identity, format information, integrity and provenance.
A surprising number of analytical errors become impossible to diagnose when the exact source bytes, decode path or channel configuration are not preserved.

At minimum, a source record should contain a content hash, original filename or external identity, container and codec information, sample rate, bit depth when meaningful, channel count, duration, decode library/version, and any normalization or transcoding event that occurred before analysis.
If the system creates an internal PCM representation, that derivative should have its own hash rather than replacing the source identity.
A useful principle is: Source identity belongs to PPE as much as to signal processing.
Without it, a later rerun cannot distinguish a changed algorithm from a changed input.

Production ML research repeatedly emphasizes the danger of undeclared dependencies and fragile pipelines; hidden technical debt often appears at boundaries where data, code and assumptions are insufficiently versioned [11].
Moodify should therefore treat source registration as the first scientific action, not as upload plumbing.

The Auditory Representation is the central integration surface of Moodify Ear.
It is where heterogeneous observations become a structured machine state that can be consumed by interpretation, judgment, reports and future learning.
A representation is not merely a flat feature vector.
For Moodify, it should preserve multiple resolutions and types of evidence.
Some properties are global, some are section-level, some are frame-level, some are pairwise between channels, and some are latent embeddings whose coordinates are not directly interpretable.
The schema must allow these forms to coexist without flattening away their identity.
The representation should contain at least temporal, spectral, dynamic, loudness, spatial/phase, transient, artifact, musical-structural, learned and uncertainty/provenance subspaces.
Each subspace should be versioned independently where useful, while the aggregate schema has its own version.

This design follows a broader lesson from representation-learning research: useful audio embeddings are task dependent, and no single representation should be assumed to dominate every downstream problem.

HEAR was explicitly designed to evaluate general-purpose audio representations across diverse tasks, reinforcing the need to test representations through their downstream utility rather than by intuition alone [4].
For Moodify, the representation layer is also an asset boundary.
New judgments can be added without re-running every sensor if the required evidence is already preserved.
New models can be compared on the same cases.
Historical reports can be regenerated against their original representation version.
A stable schema converts an internal implementation detail into a technical contract.
The contract defines what downstream components may assume and what upstream components must provide.
Each field should specify type, dimensionality, time basis, units, missing-value semantics, confidence/quality, provenance and version.
Derived quantities should identify their parents.
Learned embeddings should record model identity, checkpoint, layer selection and pooling strategy.
A representation version should change when the meaning of stored fields changes, not merely when code is refactored.
Backward compatibility can be maintained through adapters or migrations.
The important rule is that historical cases retain enough metadata to reconstruct which representation was used.

This resembles the rationale behind model cards and datasheets: machine-learning artifacts become safer and more reusable when their intended use, provenance, limitations and evaluation conditions are documented rather than left implicit [13,14].
Moodify applies the same discipline to the internal language of hearing.
The interpretation layer is where Moodify begins to move beyond analysis.
It takes the Auditory Representation and asks what the observed pattern could mean in context.

It may include musical section, neighboring windows, source format, known delivery target, local pitch/harmonic structure, likely source roles, learned similarity to reviewed cases, and the confidence of upstream components.
The interpretation layer should be able to maintain several hypotheses rather than forcing one explanation.
A high-frequency rolloff, for example, may support hypotheses involving codec history, generation bandwidth, deliberate filtering, source limitation or normal instrumentation.
The interpretation layer should rank or annotate these possibilities while preserving the underlying observation.
Auditory scene analysis is relevant here because hearing is partly a problem of organizing mixtures into meaningful streams and events rather than operating only on global statistics [5].
Music-specific context is equally important: a physical event may have different meaning in an intro, chorus, isolated vocal passage or dense ensemble.
Later evidence or human review may change the preferred hypothesis without changing the measurements that produced it.
The Judgment Engine is the first layer authorized to make explicit claims about technical risk, artistic characteristic, likely artifact, structural anomaly or uncertainty.
It is a structured record combining observations, reference basis, context, hypothesis, severity, confidence and evidence.
The engine may contain deterministic rules, probabilistic models, learned classifiers, retrieval from validated cases, or ensembles.
The architecture should permit hybrid reasoning because Ear v1 benefits from transparent rules where physics is well understood and learned components where patterns are difficult to encode manually.
The engine should not output a single universal “quality score” unless the meaning and weighting of that score are separately validated.
Instead, it should produce a set of findings whose semantics are narrow and inspectable.
A phase-risk finding can be valid even when the overall artistic quality is excellent.
Severity estimates consequence if the finding is true; confidence estimates belief that it is true.
Calibration research shows that raw neural probabilities are often not reliable estimates of empirical correctness [9].

Ear v1 should therefore preserve raw model scores and calibrated confidence separately where learned models are used. | Field | Meaning | | --- | --- | | classification | TECHNICAL_RISK / ARTISTIC_CHARACTERISTIC / LIKELY_AI_ARTIFACT / etc. | | severity | Consequence if the finding is true | | confidence | Belief that the finding is true | | reference_basis | Standard, population, paired source, case library, rule | | reason | Concise interpretation | | evidence_refs | Resolvable supporting artifacts | | provenance | Rule/model/calibration/representation versions |
Uncertainty is not an error channel outside the architecture.
It is a first-class output of the Judgment Engine.
In a rapidly changing domain such as AI-generated music, unknown patterns and distribution shifts are inevitable.
The simplest decision policy contains a reject option: Selective classification provides a formal framework for trading coverage against error by allowing uncertain examples to be rejected [10].
For Moodify, this means a case can complete successfully even when a specific judgment is withheld.
System-level uncertainty may combine model calibration, sensor agreement, evidence completeness, distance from known cases and upstream quality.
An unknown artifact family should be recorded as an unresolved anomaly rather than forced into the nearest known label.
The abstention record itself becomes a learning asset.
Repeated clusters of unresolved cases can define future research targets.
Every judgment that carries semantic authority should point backward to evidence.
The evidence layer therefore creates an inspectable graph connecting claims to observations, representations, reference models and versions.

Evidence artifacts may include waveform regions, spectrograms, loudness curves, spectral summaries, phase measurements, transient statistics, similarity examples, model outputs, calibration data and the exact rule configuration.
A high-severity finding should not survive packaging if its evidence references cannot resolve.

Explanation should distinguish what is measured from what is inferred. “Negative correlation occurred in these windows” is an observation. “This may create mono cancellation” is an interpretation. “The effect was caused by generator X” is a causal hypothesis requiring stronger evidence.
Model-card style documentation is useful at the model boundary because it encourages explicit intended use, evaluation and limitations [13].
Moodify extends that transparency into individual case-level claims.

PPE is best understood as a trust plane running through every Ear layer rather than as a separate application module.

Moodify adapts this production-readiness idea to auditory intelligence: an Ear judgment is not production-ready if it cannot prove source identity, resolve evidence, reproduce deterministic fields, expose failure states or identify the active rule/model version.
The trust plane should be mechanically enforced wherever possible.
Documentation should describe the rules, but state transitions, schema validation and test gates should prevent invalid cases from appearing complete.
The lifecycle state of a Production Case indicates what claims are currently authorized.
A case that has measurements but no validated judgment should not look equivalent to a completed report.
A failed evidence package should prevent completion even if a model prediction exists.

The exact state vocabulary may evolve, but Ear v1 should preserve a monotonic logic: source registered, analysis executed, representation produced, judgments generated, evidence resolved, report packaged, review optionally added, and learning record created.
State transitions should be caused by explicit events and should record timestamps, actor or subsystem identity, version context and failure reason.
This makes the control spine part of the scientific method: it prevents the system from silently skipping the conditions that make a result interpretable.
Moodify needs two related but different operating planes.
The *runtime plane* applies approved sensors, representations and judgment logic to production cases.

The *research plane* analyzes failures, runs experiments, tests candidate models, adjusts reference populations and evaluates proposed changes. | Runtime plane | Research plane | | --- | --- | | Approved sensors/models | Candidate sensors/models | | Frozen representation version | Schema experiments/migrations | | Approved judgment rules | Threshold/model experiments | | Production reference library | Candidate datasets / clustering | | Stable calibration | Recalibration studies | | Case generation | Failure analysis / benchmark evaluation | | No silent mutation | Produces promotion candidates | The separation protects historical reproducibility.
A research notebook may discover that a threshold should change, but the production version remains unchanged until the candidate is validated and promoted.
This is closely related to mature ML platform design, where standardized components and controlled transitions reduce fragile glue code and make training/serving behavior more manageable [15,16].
Moodify does not need industrial-scale infrastructure in v1, but it benefits from the same architectural principle: experiments and production authority should not be the same thing.

An auditory intelligence evolves through versions of many artifacts: source decoders, sensors, representation schema, learned encoders, reference datasets, judgment rules, calibration models and report schemas.
A single application version number is not enough.
A Production Case should carry a version vector or equivalent manifest.
The system can then answer questions such as: Did the judgment change because the phase sensor changed?
Because a new calibration model was promoted?
TensorFlow Serving and broader ML production platforms explicitly support model versioning and controlled serving transitions because production inference depends on more than a model file [15,17].
Ear v1 should adopt the concept at a smaller scale.
The public label “Moodify Ear v1” can therefore denote a validated compatibility envelope around a particular family of component versions rather than one monolithic binary.
Learning systems require more than model provenance.
The datasets and case collections used for thresholds, calibration, retrieval or training should carry their own documentation.
Datasheets for Datasets propose documenting motivation, composition, collection process and recommended uses so that dataset assumptions are visible to downstream users [14].
For Moodify, a benchmark or reference library should similarly record generator families, formats, languages or genres where relevant, review process, known gaps, rights status and sampling method.
This prevents a common failure mode: a reference population silently becomes a universal norm.
If an Ear threshold was calibrated mainly on one generator family or distribution pipeline, that limitation should be recoverable from the associated dataset record.
Data documentation is therefore part of the architecture of judgment, not an administrative appendix.
The first Ear must be deep without becoming operationally extravagant.

A resource-constrained architecture should separate mandatory sensors from optional expensive models and should cache reusable representations. | Tier | Purpose | Compute policy | | --- | --- | --- | | Tier 0 | Source identity, decode validation, cheap integrity checks | Always run; CPU | | Tier 1 | Core WSE/PPE deterministic measurements | Always run; CPU-first | | Tier 2 | Selected learned representations / heavier structure models | Run only when judgment value justifies cost | | Tier 3 | Research training, large comparison experiments | Offline; not required for product completion | Tier 0/1 analysis can run on CPU and produce deterministic engineering evidence.
Tier 2 may invoke larger learned encoders only when they materially improve a supported judgment.
This design avoids turning compute scarcity into architectural debt.

The canonical report should degrade gracefully: if an optional learned model is unavailable, the case can still complete with the supported deterministic findings, while clearly marking which capabilities were not executed.
The architecture should optimize for *evidence per unit of compute*, not maximum model size.
It establishes interfaces that later versions can deepen without requiring a rewrite of the entire product.
Ear v2 can improve contextual interpretation.
The same Production Case, evidence and versioning concepts remain.
Architecture is successful when new intelligence can be added as a component upgrade rather than as a new product identity.
Some properties should remain true regardless of implementation language or model family.
These invariants define the technical identity of Moodify more strongly than any UI layout.

The Moodify Ear architecture converts the phrase “AI ear” into a concrete technical system.

It begins with immutable source identity, observes through a plural sensor layer, integrates observations into a versioned Auditory Representation, interprets them in musical and technical context, produces narrow judgments with calibrated uncertainty, binds those judgments to evidence, persists them as Production Cases, and converts reviewed cases into controlled learning candidates.
PPE runs through the entire system as a trust plane.
The Intervention Lab remains separate as experimental instrumentation.
Runtime authority remains separate from research experimentation.
Versions remain explicit so that progress is reconstructable.
The result is a deliberately narrow architecture.
It does not attempt to generate, mix, master, distribute or trade music.
It solves a prior problem: *how can a machine build reliable knowledge from sound?* That is the architecture of Moodify Ear v1.

Before a machine can infer structure, context or intention, it must establish a disciplined account of what physically happened in the signal.
Wave-Spectral Evolution, or WSE, is the framework for that account.
WSE treats an audio file as a time-varying physical record whose amplitude, spectrum, dynamics, spatial relationships and transient behavior evolve continuously.
Its central question is deliberately narrow: *What happened in the sound?* It does not initially ask whether the event is good, bad, artistic, accidental or generated by a particular model.
A reliable Ear needs a sensor layer that can survive changing models and changing artistic conventions.
If physical observations are stable and versioned, higher-level interpretations can evolve without losing the evidence that produced them.
It is a coordinate system for hearing the physical signal.

The short-time Fourier transform, STFT, applies a window w[n] around successive time positions and computes a Fourier transform for each frame: The STFT produces a two-dimensional time-frequency representation X(m,k).
Its magnitude is commonly visualized as a spectrogram.
This is one of the most important instruments in Moodify Ear because it reveals how spectral energy evolves.
Window length creates a fundamental engineering tradeoff.
Longer windows improve frequency discrimination but smear fast events in time.
Shorter windows localize transients but blur closely spaced frequencies.
The choice is not neutral: different WSE questions require different resolutions.
A single spectrogram configuration should therefore not be treated as the canonical truth.
Ear v1 should support at least two resolutions: a transient-oriented short window and a spectral-structure-oriented longer window.
More advanced versions can use a multiresolution bank.
Framing a finite segment implicitly multiplies the signal by a window.
A rectangular cut creates sharp boundaries and can spread energy across frequency bins.
Smooth windows reduce leakage at the cost of other resolution properties.

The key principle is not to select one universally optimal window.

Human auditory perception does not use one uniform time-frequency scale.

Music itself also contains phenomena at very different durations: sub-millisecond waveform details, tens-of-milliseconds transients, hundreds-of-milliseconds syllables and beats, multi-second phrases, and whole-track dynamic arcs.

Constant-Q and related nonstationary transforms provide another useful resolution strategy.
Their frequency spacing is approximately logarithmic, offering higher relative frequency resolution at low frequencies and time resolution that changes with frequency.

Many of its first validations are physical invariance and controlled-sensitivity tests.
Its output is a structured set of physical observations, not a verdict on the music.
The transition can be represented as: This boundary must remain visible in code.
A spectral sensor should not label a song “bad.” A phase module should not decide that width is inappropriate.
A loudness meter should not invent a universal artistic target.
The same physical observations can later support distribution compliance, artistic analysis, AI-artifact research, recommendation or intervention without rewriting the sensing layer.
WSE can be summarized by ten principles. **1.
The physical signal comes first.** Semantic claims must be grounded in reproducible observations. **2.
Time is preserved.** Global summaries are derived from local evidence, not the reverse. **3.
Resolution is task-dependent.** No single STFT window or transform is universal. **4.
Magnitude is incomplete without phase.** Stereo and reconstruction behavior require relational information. **5.
Loudness is not amplitude.** Peak, energy and perceptual loudness serve different questions. **6.
Dynamics are multi-scale.** Micro-, meso- and macro-dynamics should remain distinguishable. **7.
Bandwidth evidence is not an artifact label.** Physical detection precedes causal interpretation. **8.
Residuals require explicit references.** Difference plots are meaningful only when the comparison is defined. **9.
Figures are evidence.** Every visualization should answer a technical question and carry provenance. **10.
WSE does not judge alone.** It contributes the physical state from which the Ear can later understand.
With these rules, WSE becomes the sensory substrate of Moodify Ear v1: narrow enough to be testable, rich enough to support future intelligence.
Wave-Spectral Evolution gives Moodify Ear a physical memory of sound.
It preserves how amplitude, frequency, dynamics, transients, spatial relations, phase, bandwidth and residual structures change through time.
This memory is not yet hearing in the full sense developed earlier in the book.
It is the material from which hearing can be built.
The interpretation and judgment layers will convert observations into hypotheses.
Learning will determine which physical patterns matter across cases.
The importance of WSE is therefore foundational: before a machine can understand sound, it must be able to remember what the sound actually did.

Modern systems commonly separate local beat activation from a temporal decoding model.
Recurrent networks and dynamic Bayesian networks have been used successfully for joint beat and downbeat tracking [3].
Transformer-based approaches have extended this idea with longer-context modeling [4].

This reduces sensitivity to small timing variations and provides a musically meaningful axis.
Chroma, timbral embeddings, spectral summaries, loudness and learned features can all be pooled by beat or bar.
Music-structure systems frequently exploit beat-synchronous or bar-synchronous features because repetition is more visible when compared on a common musical grid [5-7].

Structural aggregation is a view, not a replacement.
One of the most useful ideas in music-structure analysis is the self-similarity matrix.
Given a feature sequence z_1, ..., z_T, the matrix compares each time position with every other position: Repeated sections appear as block or diagonal structures.
Novelty boundaries can emerge where the local similarity pattern changes.
Self-similarity matrices have become a standard representation for music structure analysis and have supported both classical and learned segmentation methods [5-9].

For Moodify, SSMs are valuable because they expose recurrence without requiring a fixed vocabulary of “verse” and “chorus.” The Ear can first recognize that sections repeat, then attach functional labels only when evidence supports them.
A structural boundary is a hypothesis that the musical state changes around time t.
Novelty-based methods compare the self-similarity pattern before and after a candidate point.
Peaks in the novelty function can suggest transitions.
Modern work also learns representations and kernels directly for structure analysis, showing that the feature space itself can be optimized for segmentation [8,9].
MSE should store boundary confidence and scale.
A local phrase boundary is not equivalent to a track-level section boundary.
Multi-level structure is preferable to a single segmentation when the data supports it.
Automatic structure analysis often aims to partition a track into segments and optionally assign functional labels such as verse, chorus, bridge or solo.
Surveys of audio-based music structure analysis emphasize that segmentation and labeling remain challenging because musical form is diverse and annotation itself can be ambiguous [10].

The Harmonix Set provides beat, downbeat and functional segmentation annotations for hundreds of popular tracks, illustrating how structural ground truth can be constructed for learning and evaluation [11].
Ear v1 should avoid pretending that every track follows a fixed pop form.

Harmony can be represented in a compact way by folding pitches separated by octaves into twelve pitch classes.
Chroma features have long been used because they are relatively robust to timbre and preserve information relevant to harmonic progression [12].
A chroma vector at time t summarizes energy associated with pitch classes C, C-sharp, ..., B.
Variants can be derived from spectrograms, constant-Q representations or learned pitch-class models [12,13].
It may contain overtones, melodic tones and non-harmonic energy.
Moodify should preserve this distinction just as WSE separates spectra from judgments.
Automatic chord recognition maps audio to symbolic harmonic labels.
Two decades of research show both the usefulness and the difficulty of this task, with chroma representations, temporal models and learned features playing central roles [14,15].
For Ear v1, chord estimation should be treated as contextual evidence rather than a required truth source.
A coarse harmonic-state representation may already be enough to detect section repetition, modulation regions or changes in harmonic density.
If chord labels are emitted, they should carry confidence and vocabulary identity.
Different chord taxonomies can produce different “correct” labels for the same sonority.
Predominant-melody algorithms estimate a pitch trajectory corresponding to the perceptually dominant melodic line.
Such systems must separate candidate pitch contours from accompaniment and choose among competing trajectories.

A pitch trajectory can be represented as frequency f_0(t) or a symbolic pitch value: Pitch confidence is essential because polyphonic mixtures, breathy singing, distortion and generated timbral artifacts can make F0 ambiguous.
Moodify should distinguish “no confident pitch” from “silence.” Melodic contours can help align repeated phrases, lyrics and structural sections even when full note transcription is unreliable.
Automatic Music Transcription (AMT) attempts to convert audio into note events with pitch, onset, duration and sometimes instrument identity.
Multi-instrument transcription remains a difficult core problem of music understanding [16].
Sequence-to-sequence systems such as MT3 demonstrate that a unified Transformer can transcribe multiple instruments and tasks across several datasets [16].
More recent work continues to push general multi-instrument transcription, but real-world polyphonic music remains challenging.
Moodify Ear v1 should therefore use transcription opportunistically.
A MIDI-like event layer can enrich MSE when confidence is sufficient, but the entire Ear must not depend on perfect transcription.

Automatic lyrics alignment is difficult because singing differs from speech in duration, pitch range, pronunciation and accompaniment.

A finished mix is a superposition of sources.
MSE does not need perfect source separation to infer that a vocal, drums or bass-like role is active, but source-aware context can greatly improve interpretation.
Music source separation aims to estimate constituent sources such as vocals, drums, bass and accompaniment.
Waveform-domain Demucs and later Hybrid Transformer Demucs demonstrate how learned systems can separate music into stems with increasing quality [20,21].
A separated stem is an estimate, not the original studio track.
Bleeding and separation artifacts can contaminate downstream measurements.

Four stems - vocals, drums, bass and other - are useful but coarse.
MoisesDB introduced a dataset with a more detailed hierarchical taxonomy of musical sources, illustrating the demand for finer structural descriptions [22].
A future MSE can represent roles hierarchically: vocals -> lead/backing; drums -> kick/snare/cymbals; harmonic -> guitar/keys; low-frequency -> bass/sub; effects and ambience.
Ear v1 does not need full separation at this resolution, but its schema should not prevent later expansion.
Hierarchical roles matter because physical judgments are source dependent.
Low-frequency accumulation in a bass stem is different from low-frequency leakage in a vocal estimate.
Repetition, hierarchy and cross-layer relations make it naturally graph-like.
Moodify can represent structural entities as nodes and relations as edges: Nodes may include beats, bars, phrases, sections, lyric lines, note events and source-role intervals.
Edges may encode contains, precedes, repeats, aligns-with, overlaps, harmonically-similar-to or derived-from.
This graph provides a powerful bridge to evidence.
A WSE finding can attach to a time range; the graph can identify which section, lyric line and source-role hypotheses overlap that range.
The graph need not be a graph database in v1.
The architectural concept is what matters: structural relations should be queryable rather than flattened into one label array.

Without MSE, the Ear sees a change in short-term loudness.
With MSE, it can know that the jump coincides with a chorus downbeat, recurs at the next chorus and is accompanied by increased instrumentation.

This evidence shifts the interpretation from “unexpected discontinuity” toward “structural arrangement change.” Conversely, a spectral discontinuity in the middle of a stable repeated phrase, absent in parallel repetitions, may become more suspicious.

One simple propagation principle is: The exact combination rule may differ by model, but the conceptual rule is fixed: downstream confidence cannot ignore uncertainty in a required upstream premise.

The Judgment Engine can consume physical and structural states together without treating either as universal truth.
A machine begins to hear musical structure when it can use these relations to change what it concludes about the same physical signal.
MSE can be summarized by ten principles. **1.
Musical time is relational.** Seconds remain necessary, but beats, bars, phrases and sections create the relevant context. **2.
Onsets are not beats.** Local acoustic events and latent metrical structure are separate inference problems. **3.
Repetition is primary evidence.** Similarity relationships can be useful even when semantic section labels are uncertain. **4.
Symbolic output is a hypothesis.** Chords, MIDI notes and scores carry provenance and confidence. **5.
Lyrics are timed structure.** Known-text alignment and transcription are different tasks. **6.
Separated stems are estimates.** Source separation must propagate model identity and uncertainty. **7.
Structure is multi-level.** Phrase, section and whole-track form should not be collapsed into one scale. **8.
WSE and MSE share one timeline.** Physical findings and musical entities must be cross-queryable. **9.
Structural uncertainty propagates.** Downstream judgments cannot pretend their premises are certain. **10.
MSE exists to improve hearing.** A structural feature is valuable when it changes interpretation, evidence or learning.
These principles keep MSE narrow enough for Ear v1 while leaving a path toward deeper musical understanding.
WSE gives Moodify a physical memory of sound.

Beats establish pulse; downbeats and bars establish meter; repetition and self-similarity reveal form; chroma and pitch expose harmonic and melodic relations; lyrics, transcription and source roles provide additional structural layers.
None of these estimates should be treated as infallible.

When aligned to the same timeline and carried with confidence, they allow the Judgment Engine to compare like with like, recognize expected variation, localize anomalies musically and learn from repeated structure.
The question of MSE is therefore not whether a machine can produce a perfect score.
It is whether the machine can know enough about musical organization to hear the physical signal more intelligently.
That is the role of Musical-Structural Engineering in Moodify Ear v1.

**Technical Monographs - Volume I** **Chapter VII - PPE - Making Hearing Trustworthy** **August 2026** > A hearing result becomes knowledge only when identity, evidence, state and lineage survive the run that produced it.
A machine can produce a correct result and still be untrustworthy.

The problem appears whenever the system cannot prove which source it heard, which configuration it used, which model generated a finding, which evidence supported the decision, whether a failure was silently ignored, or whether the same case can be reconstructed later.
Production Process Engineering, or PPE, exists to solve this second-order problem.
PPE asks: *How was this hearing produced reliably?* PPE does not make the Ear more sensitive in the immediate perceptual sense.
A result that cannot be identified, reproduced, reviewed and inherited is an isolated event.
A result with stable identity, provenance and closure can become institutional knowledge.
For Moodify Ear v1, trust is therefore an engineered property rather than a feeling.
It is constructed from identity, state, provenance, evidence, reproducibility, failure semantics, authority boundaries, versioning and controlled promotion.
PPE should not be implemented as one administrative module placed beside the auditory pipeline.
It is a transversal trust plane that crosses every layer of the Ear.
The trust state T of a case depends on source identity, run identity, version identity, evidence completeness, lifecycle state, failure state, authority state and reproducibility status.
A single green “success” flag is too weak to represent these dimensions.
This architecture reflects a broader lesson from production machine learning: model code is only a small fraction of the real system.
Data dependencies, serving, monitoring, configuration, validation and surrounding infrastructure often dominate production complexity [1,2].

PPE makes those dependencies visible at the unit of the Production Case. | Without PPE | Failure of trust | | --- | --- | | No source hash | Cannot prove which audio was analyzed | | No run identity | Cannot reconstruct which execution produced the result | | Mutable defaults | Same command may mean different things over time | | No evidence index | Judgment cannot be audited | | One success flag | Partial/failed/blocked cases look complete | | Silent feedback mutation | Historical behavior cannot be reproduced | | No migration contract | Old cases silently change meaning |

“Moodify Ear v1” is a public compatibility label, not a sufficient technical version.
Internally the Ear is composed of many independently changing artifacts.
A representation-schema migration may change downstream values even when a model is unchanged.
A calibration update may alter confidence while leaving classification unchanged.
A new decoder may slightly alter sensor measurements.
Model Cards formalize the idea that a model should carry documented intended use, evaluation and limitations [4].
Datasheets extend similar discipline to datasets [5].
PPE generalizes this documentation approach to the entire hearing stack.
A case should pass through explicit lifecycle states rather than jump from “uploaded” to “done.” State is not UI decoration; it determines which claims the system is authorized to make.
A state transition should be triggered by an explicit event and should record timestamp, actor or subsystem, prior state, next state and reason.
Invalid transitions should be rejected mechanically.

The exact vocabulary may evolve, but the logic should distinguish creation, source registration, specification, analysis, validation, approval where required, execution, verification, packaging and completion.
Failed and blocked branches should remain first-class.
This turns the control spine into part of the scientific method.

A case cannot become complete merely because one model returned a score. | State class | Meaning | | --- | --- | | in-progress | Required work remains and the case may advance | | awaiting-authority | Technical work is ready but human/explicit authority is required | | failed | A required operation could not satisfy its contract | | blocked | External dependency prevents valid progress | | cancelled | Explicit decision ended the case | | completed | All mandatory gates and packaging requirements passed |
Terminal states determine how the rest of the organization interprets a case. “Complete,” “failed,” “blocked,” “cancelled” and “partial” are not interchangeable.
A completed case should mean that all mandatory evidence, validation and packaging gates for the selected case type have passed.
A failed case should mean that the system attempted a required operation and could not satisfy its contract.
A blocked case should identify an unmet external dependency or authority decision.
Precise terminal states improve automation because downstream systems can distinguish “retry,” “ask a human,” “investigate a defect,” and “accept as final.”

A reviewed case should not directly mutate production behavior.

Promotion is a separate event that requires validation against regression cases and benchmark policy.
The production artifact receives a new version only after the promotion gate passes.
This pattern prevents online feedback from becoming uncontrolled drift.
It also preserves historical truth: an old case can always be reconstructed under the Ear version that actually heard it.
The distinction between feedback and promotion is one of PPE's most important contributions to a learning Ear.
Not every code change should create a new public Ear generation, but changes that alter meaning must be visible.

PPE can classify changes as: | Change class | Example | Expected policy | | --- | --- | --- | | non-semantic | refactor/logging/UI layout | no case-meaning change expected | | compatible feature | new optional evidence artifact | old cases remain valid | | semantic minor | threshold/calibration update | new internal version + regression | | schema/model major | representation meaning changes | migration/compatibility review | | breaking | old contract cannot be supported | explicit deprecation + archive reader | The exact numbering scheme can remain project-specific.
What matters is that consumers can tell whether a change is expected to preserve case semantics.
A representation-schema change deserves particular care because many downstream artifacts may depend on it.
Migration should never silently reinterpret historical values.
An accumulating system must eventually replace old schemas, sensors and APIs.
Deprecation is therefore part of durability, not evidence of failure.
A safe migration plan should identify old version, new version, compatibility strategy, data transformation, validation method, rollback path and authority owner.
Historical Production Cases should remain readable under their original contracts even if the live runtime has moved forward.
Adapters or archive readers may be preferable to rewriting every historical case into a new interpretation.
Failures should be recoverable without creating duplicate authority.
If a run stops after analysis but before packaging, the system should be able to resume or replay from a known checkpoint.
Replay requires clear separation between idempotent operations and operations that create external side effects.
Ear-only Phase I simplifies this substantially because listening is predominantly read/compute/write rather than act-on-world.
A resumed run should record that recovery occurred and which artifacts were reused.
If recomputation changes a deterministic artifact unexpectedly, the case should surface a reproducibility problem rather than silently overwrite it.

Trust infrastructure can become counterproductive if every engineering action requires manual paperwork.
PPE should therefore automate provenance collection wherever possible.
Hashes, version manifests, run IDs, timestamps, environment fingerprints, evidence indexes and state transitions can be generated mechanically.
Humans should spend authority only where judgment or governance actually requires it.
This follows an important systems principle: the safest control is often the one encoded in the mechanism rather than remembered as a procedure.
Not every finding requires the same assurance level.
An informational spectral note may tolerate lower evidential burden than a high-severity technical-risk judgment or a future action that modifies assets.

PPE can define assurance as a function of consequence: Risk management frameworks such as NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 23894 emphasize that governance should be proportional to context, impact and uncertainty [8,9].
Moodify can apply the principle narrowly: higher semantic or operational consequence requires stronger validation, evidence and authority.
This avoids both extremes - treating every observation as safety-critical and treating every model output as equally harmless.
A reproducible run should record environment identity without leaking secrets.
API keys, private tokens and user credentials must never become case evidence.
PPE should distinguish reproducibility metadata from sensitive runtime secrets.
Environment manifests can record dependency versions, operating system, hardware class and configuration fingerprints while excluding secret values.
Least privilege also applies to storage: a component that only needs to read source audio should not automatically receive permission to modify learning rules or publish reports.
Security therefore protects the integrity of hearing as well as user data.
Resource use is part of reproducibility and product design.
A hearing capability that works only with unbounded compute is not production-stable.
Each case can record approximate CPU/GPU time, wall-clock latency, peak memory and optional model calls.
These values do not determine correctness, but they allow Ear versions to be compared on evidence efficiency.
For a resource-constrained Ear v1, the target is not minimum cost at any price.
It is maximum trustworthy evidence per unit of compute.
The first Ear does not require an enterprise-scale MLOps platform.
More sophisticated orchestration, distributed tracing, remote feature stores or continuous training can wait until scale creates a real need.
The principle is the same as the Ear-only product strategy: narrow infrastructure, deep guarantees.
PPE succeeds when such violations become visible and classifiable rather than silently accepted.
PPE creates the interface between production and research: The loop is deliberately closed.
A production case does not disappear after the report is shown.
Review turns it into evidence about the Ear itself.
Validated learning changes theory, rules, calibration or models.
The next case is therefore heard by a system that carries forward institutional memory.
This is how Moodify becomes more than software that processes independent uploads.
The Ear becomes an accumulating research system.
PPE can be summarized by twelve principles. **1.
Every hearing event has identity.** Source, case and run are separate and stable. **2.
Configuration is evidence.** Defaults that affect meaning must be materialized and versioned. **3.
State authorizes claims.** A case cannot skip semantic gates simply because computation succeeded. **4.
Failure is preserved.** Missing or failed evidence never becomes a fabricated zero or success. **5.
Reproducibility has classes.** Bitwise, tolerance and statistical reproducibility are different contracts. **6.
Evidence is an object.** Artifacts carry hashes, producers and relationships. **7.
Authority is explicit.** Observe, recommend, approve and execute are different permissions. **8.
Learning is not mutation.** Feedback creates candidates; promotion changes production. **9.
Historical meaning is protected.** Migration does not silently rewrite old cases. **10.
Closure is governed.** Complete, failed, blocked and cancelled have exact semantics. **11.
Trust scales with consequence.** Higher-impact claims require stronger evidence and validation. **12.
Mechanisms beat memory.** Controls should be automated wherever possible.
Together these principles turn reliability into an architectural property of the Ear.
WSE and MSE make it possible for Moodify to observe and contextualize sound.
PPE makes those observations durable enough to become knowledge.

A trustworthy Ear knows what it heard, which system heard it, how the result was produced, what evidence supported the judgment, where uncertainty remains, which failures occurred, who held authority, and whether the case can be reconstructed later.
This discipline may appear orthogonal to intelligence, but it is what allows intelligence to compound.
Without PPE, each successful analysis is a demonstration.
With PPE, each validated case becomes part of a reproducible lineage from Ear v1 to every later version.
PPE therefore answers the third foundational question of Moodify Ear: not only *can the machine hear?*, but *can we trust what it says it heard?*

A compact conceptual form for Auditory Representation v1 is: Z_WSE contains physical time-frequency, dynamic, spatial and artifact evidence.
Z_MSE contains musical time, sections, repetition, harmonic/pitch, lyric and source-role hypotheses.
Z_L contains learned embeddings or model-derived latent states.
U contains uncertainty and data-quality fields.
G contains relations between temporal, structural and evidential entities.
A production Ear should not force every kind of information through one latent bottleneck when the original interpretable evidence remains valuable.
Redundancy is acceptable when its semantics are explicit.

The WSE subspace provides the physical state described in Chapter V.
It should include both compact descriptors and evidence-preserving trajectories.
Each local field should identify its temporal support, units, analysis parameters, quality state and source sensor.
A spectral slope without the frequency range and transform settings is incomplete.
A correlation value without window support is ambiguous.
The WSE subspace is therefore not just a dictionary of numbers.
It is a set of typed observations with boundaries.
The MSE subspace adds the musical organization developed in Chapter VI.
Structural entities should be interval-based where possible.
A section is represented not only by the label “chorus,” but by start/end time, stable section identity, repetition group, functional-label confidence and the evidence/model that produced it.
Symbolic content such as chords or MIDI-like note events should record vocabulary or transcription-model identity.
The Ear must know whether a note came from a human-authored score, an aligned generator output or automatic transcription.

Large-scale self-supervised and supervised audio models demonstrate that useful information can be learned directly from sound. wav2vec 2.0 showed the power of self-supervised representation learning for speech [1].
PANNs and AST demonstrated broad transfer from large-scale audio recognition [2,3].
Audio-MAE and BEATs further developed masked/self-supervised audio pretraining [4,5].
MERT introduced music-specific self-supervised representations [6].
Moodify should treat these models as additional senses, not as the entire Ear.
A learned embedding can capture semantic or timbral structure that handcrafted descriptors miss, but its coordinates may be difficult to interpret and may not preserve engineering-sensitive details.

A learned feature record should therefore include: | Field | Why it matters | | --- | --- | | model_id / checkpoint | identifies the actual encoder | | input view | waveform, spectrogram, stem, excerpt, etc. | | layer | different layers encode different information | | pooling | mean/CLS/frame sequence changes semantics | | time support | global vs local embedding | | normalization | distance metrics depend on transform | | quality/status | model may fail or be out-of-domain | The representation may store several embeddings for different purposes.
A general-audio embedding, a music-specific embedding and an artifact-specific embedding need not be collapsed into one vector.
HEAR and MARBLE reinforce this task-dependent view: representations should be evaluated by downstream performance across meaningful tasks rather than assumed to be universally optimal [7,8].

section: 9. Hybrid Representation Is a Deliberate Choice
claim: Moodify Ear v1 adopts a hybrid representation because no single representation family satisfies all requirements. | Component | Strength | Weakness | | --- | --- | --- | | engineering descriptors | interpretable, reproducible | limited semantic capacity | | MSE structure | musically meaningful context | estimation errors / ambiguity | | learned embeddings | rich pattern sensitivity | opaque / task-dependent | | retrieval links | case-based evidence | depends on corpus quality | | relation graph | explicit compositional context | schema complexity | Handcrafted physical descriptors offer direct interpretability and deterministic behavior.
