section: 9. Hybrid Representation Is a Deliberate Choice
claim: It is an explicit response to the heterogeneity of hearing.
If the vocal separator fails, Moodify does not suddenly know that vocal energy is zero.
If beat confidence is too low, the representation should not fabricate a beat grid.
Each optional field therefore requires a status such as PRESENT, NOT_RUN, FAILED, NOT_APPLICABLE, or INSUFFICIENT_CONFIDENCE.
This distinction prevents a common data-engineering failure in which null, zero and failure are conflated.
Downstream judgments can then reason about whether required premises actually exist.
PPE uses the same status to decide whether a finding is allowed to become authoritative.
Uncertainty is not only a final judgment property.
Sensors, alignments, structural boundaries and learned states have their own uncertainty.

Auditory Representation v1 therefore attaches local quality/confidence to representation elements: A chorus boundary might be estimated at 62.4 seconds with moderate confidence and a tolerance region.
A pitch trajectory might be highly reliable in the verse and unreliable in a noisy bridge.
A source-role interval might be only probabilistic.
This allows downstream uncertainty to be propagated instead of invented at the end of the pipeline.
Two identical numeric values may not mean the same thing if they were produced by different sensor versions, windows, models or calibration policies.
Provenance is therefore part of representation semantics.
W3C PROV formalizes relationships among entities, activities and agents for general provenance tracking [9].
Moodify can use a simpler project-native structure while preserving the same principle: important representation fields should identify what produced them.
Provenance also supports selective recomputation.
If one sensor changes, the system can identify which representation fields and judgments need regeneration.
Auditory Representation v1 should be machine-readable and strongly typed enough to reject ambiguous data.

A conceptual record may contain: | Top-level field | Contents | | --- | --- | | identity | source_id, case_id, representation_id, run_id | | timeline | sample/second coordinates + musical mappings | | wse | physical observations and trajectories | | mse | metrical/section/harmonic/lyric/source structure | | learned | versioned latent representations | | relations | containment/repetition/alignment/evidence edges | | uncertainty | field-level confidence/status/quality | | provenance | producer versions/config/input references | | summary | derived section/track aggregates with lineage | The exact serialization format can be JSON, MessagePack, Parquet or another project-native form.
The contract should define required fields, units, status vocabulary, version rules and references.
A schema validator should run before a representation can become part of a completed Production Case.
Audio software frequently mixes linear amplitude, power, dBFS, LUFS, normalized frequency and hertz without enough metadata.
Moodify should make units explicit at the representation boundary.
A typed value pairs the numeric value with unit, support, reference and producer.
This may seem verbose, but it prevents silent errors when multiple modules are combined.
Frequency normalized to Nyquist is not interchangeable with hertz.
Sample peak in dBFS is not integrated loudness in LUFS.
Correlation is dimensionless but window-dependent.
The schema should encode these differences rather than rely on developer memory.

Auditory Representation v1 can be summarized by twelve principles. **1.
Representation is a language.** It defines what the Ear can state internally. **2.
One vector is insufficient.** Physical, structural, learned and evidential states coexist. **3.
Time is primary.** Global summaries derive from local states. **4.
Physical and musical time coexist.** Seconds remain ground truth while beats/sections add context. **5.
Missingness is explicit.** Failure, absence and zero are different. **6.
Uncertainty begins locally.** Confidence propagates rather than appearing only at the final judgment. **7.
Provenance is semantic.** Producer identity and version affect meaning. **8.
Units are typed.** Numeric values without units/support are incomplete. **9.
Aggregation preserves lineage.** Summaries remain connected to evidence. **10.
Learned features are additional senses.** They complement rather than replace interpretable state. **11.
Versions protect history.** New schemas expand knowledge without rewriting old cases. **12.
The representation serves judgment and learning.** Fields earn their place by making the Ear more reliable, explainable or extensible.
Provenance records how each element was produced.
Relations connect time, structure, evidence and cases.
The Auditory Representation is the point at which isolated measurements become a coherent machine state without yet becoming a final judgment.
It is the substrate from which Interpretation, Judgment, Evidence, Retrieval and Learning can operate.
A machine begins to learn to hear not when it stores more audio, but when it can preserve what it heard in a form that can be compared, questioned, corrected and reused.
Auditory Representation v1 is the first such form for Moodify Ear.

PPE requires regression and benchmark validation before the new judgment family/version becomes production authority.
The Ear therefore learns at two speeds: cases accumulate continuously, while production judgment changes occur discretely through validated releases.
A single global accuracy score would hide the fact that direct physical findings and causal artifact hypotheses have very different difficulty and consequence.
The Intervention Lab can strengthen judgment validation because the transformation is known.
If a low-pass filter is deliberately applied, the Ear's bandwidth judgment can be compared with causal ground truth.
Such experiments are especially valuable for establishing monotonicity: as intervention strength increases, evidence and confidence should change in a predictable direction over a useful range.
Not every judgment can be validated through synthetic intervention, but the families that can should use it.
A robust judgment should respond to relevant changes and remain stable to irrelevant ones.

For finding J, construct a relevant transformation T_r and irrelevant transformation T_i: If a bandwidth finding changes when file metadata changes but not when the spectrum changes, the model has learned the wrong cue.
If a phase-risk judgment responds to channel-phase manipulation but remains stable to filename changes, its behavior is more plausible.
Counterfactual testing is one defense against shortcut learning.
Ear v1 does not need a universal end-to-end judge.
The objective is to establish a decision architecture that later models can enter without changing the semantic contract.
A useful Ear v1 target is not dozens of speculative categories, but a compact set of reliable judgment families.
Some, such as low-frequency accumulation or transient damage, require stronger contextual reference than clipping.
The list should be treated as an engineering proposal rather than a permanent ontology.
A family enters production only when its evidence contract and benchmark pass.
The Auditory Report is the human projection of the Judgment Engine.

It should answer four questions for every supported finding: **What did Moodify hear?** The concise judgment. **Where?** Time range and structural context. **Why?** Evidence and reference basis. **How sure?** Confidence, uncertainty and any limitations.
A section titled “Unresolved / insufficient evidence” can be more informative than forcing every observation into a problem list.
The transition from measurement to judgment can be summarized by twelve principles. **1.
Judgment is semantic authority.** It carries more responsibility than measurement. **2.
Interpretation precedes verdict.** Competing hypotheses may remain unresolved. **3.
Every normative claim has a reference.** Thresholds without provenance are not knowledge. **4.
Belief and consequence differ.** Confidence and severity remain separate. **5.
Raw probability is not calibrated confidence.** Reliability must be measured. **6.
Error costs are judgment-specific.** False positives and false negatives do not always matter equally. **7.
Abstention is intelligence.** Coverage must be traded against error consciously. **8.
Context can reverse meaning.** MSE changes how WSE is interpreted. **9.
Retrieval supplies case evidence, not automatic truth.** Similarity must identify its view and corpus. **10.
Hybrid reasoning is legitimate.** Rules, models and cases can coexist under one contract. **11.
Explanation is layered.** Observation, interpretation and causal hypothesis are not interchangeable. **12.
Judgments learn through validated cases.** Production authority changes only through promotion.
Auditory Representation gives Moodify a language for what it heard.
The Judgment Engine gives that language semantic responsibility.
The transition is not a single classifier call.

It begins with references, maintains hypotheses, combines physical and structural evidence, calibrates confidence, separates severity from belief, recognizes unknowns, allows abstention, retrieves prior cases and records a versioned JudgmentRecord.
This is the point at which Moodify Ear becomes useful as an intelligence rather than merely an analyzer.
It can make claims, but it can also show why those claims deserve trust and where their limits lie.
A machine does not learn to hear by producing more numbers.
It begins to learn to hear when it can decide what the numbers mean without forgetting that it may be wrong.

A common distinction in probabilistic machine learning separates aleatoric uncertainty from epistemic uncertainty [1,2]. | Type | Meaning | Example in Moodify | | --- | --- | --- | | aleatoric | ambiguity/noise intrinsic to observation | two overlapping sources make local pitch unclear | | epistemic | system lacks knowledge | new artifact pattern absent from validated cases | Aleatoric uncertainty reflects ambiguity or noise intrinsic to the observation.
If a dense stereo mix genuinely contains overlapping sources that make one event ambiguous, more training data may not fully remove that ambiguity.
Epistemic uncertainty reflects lack of knowledge in the model or system.
If the Ear has never encountered a new generator family, uncertainty may be reduced through new validated cases and model updates.
Moodify should not overclaim a perfect decomposition.

The distinction is still useful because it changes the learning response: irreducible ambiguity suggests abstention or richer observation, while epistemic uncertainty suggests research, new cases or new representation.
Ear v1 should represent uncertainty as a structured record rather than a scalar confidence field.
The record identifies where uncertainty originates, whether it is local or global, how it was estimated, what evidence is missing, and what action is permitted.
A final confidence number may be derived for reporting, but the structured form remains authoritative.
This makes uncertainty auditable in the same way that evidence is auditable.

A well-calibrated confidence q should approximately satisfy: Expected Calibration Error, reliability diagrams, Brier score and negative log-likelihood are common tools for measuring probabilistic quality [3-5].
Each summarizes different properties and none should be treated as universally sufficient.
Calibration must be measured per judgment family because clipping detection, phase-risk judgment and AI-artifact attribution have different class balance and difficulty.
Calibration should also be re-evaluated when the generator population or reference corpus changes.

A confidence model that was valid in August 2026 may not remain valid after the audio distribution shifts. | Metric | What it reveals | | --- | --- | | reliability diagram | observed correctness vs reported confidence | | ECE | weighted average calibration gap across confidence bins | | Brier score | squared probabilistic error | | negative log-likelihood | penalizes low probability assigned to true outcomes | | coverage at confidence | how much of the domain remains after thresholding |

Calibration measured on familiar data can degrade when the deployment distribution changes.
Ovadia et al. systematically showed that predictive uncertainty under dataset shift can fail in ways that are not visible on the training distribution [6].
Moodify is especially exposed because AI-generated music is not stationary.
Generator architectures, codecs, release workflows and stylistic conventions can change rapidly.
The Ear should therefore treat domain shift as an operational condition, not a rare academic edge case.
A case can be physically valid yet statistically unfamiliar.

Hybrid Judgment Engine components may disagree.
A deterministic rule may flag an event while a learned model does not.
Two learned encoders may rank different hypotheses.
WSE may indicate a discontinuity while MSE shows a repeated section boundary.
Disagreement should be modeled explicitly: Ensemble methods often improve predictive uncertainty by exposing variation across independently trained models [11].
In Moodify, disagreement can also occur across fundamentally different evidence families, which may be even more informative.
The system should not hide conflict by averaging everything into one smooth score.
A reviewer may need to see that the physical evidence is strong but the causal classification is contested.
Combining evidence is difficult because many sensors are correlated.
Spectral centroid, high-band energy and spectral tilt may all respond to the same physical change.
Treating them as independent can produce exaggerated certainty.

A fusion policy should therefore group evidence by dependency: The Ear can combine within groups conservatively and give greater weight to genuinely complementary evidence such as physical bandwidth evidence plus repeated-case similarity plus structural context.
This is another reason to preserve provenance: dependency is easier to reason about when the origin of each signal is visible.

Deep ensembles approximate epistemic uncertainty by training multiple models and observing variation in their predictions [11].
Conceptually: The predictive mean can support the central decision, while variance or disagreement estimates model uncertainty.
Ensembles are computationally expensive, so Ear v1 may reserve them for difficult judgment families or offline calibration.
Resource cost should be weighed against uncertainty value, consistent with the Ear's evidence-per-compute principle.
Monte Carlo dropout and related approximate Bayesian methods provide another way to estimate predictive variability by sampling model behavior at inference [12].
These methods are useful research tools but should not be treated as automatically calibrated uncertainty.
Empirical validation on Moodify's cases remains necessary.
Ear v1 can support such methods experimentally without making them a mandatory runtime dependency.

As the acceptance threshold rises, coverage falls and average error among accepted cases often falls.
This relationship can be visualized as a risk-coverage curve.
Ear v1 should benchmark each judgment family over multiple thresholds instead of selecting one threshold without context.
This shows how much coverage must be sacrificed to achieve a target error rate.
A family that only becomes reliable at extremely low coverage may remain research-only.
Traditional accuracy treats abstention as missing output.
Moodify needs a metric that recognizes appropriate refusal.

A useful evaluation can classify cases into: correct accepted judgment, incorrect accepted judgment, appropriate abstention, unnecessary abstention and unsupported forced judgment. | Outcome | Meaning | | --- | --- | | correct accepted | Ear judged and was right | | incorrect accepted | dangerous overreach | | appropriate abstention | case was genuinely unsupported/ambiguous | | unnecessary abstention | Ear could have judged reliably but refused | | forced unsupported judgment | semantic failure even if runtime succeeded | This taxonomy lets the team optimize for trustworthy utility rather than raw answer count.
The long-term objective is not to minimize abstention.

claim: This turns human attention into a scarce resource allocated by epistemic need.
When human review is expensive, cases can be prioritized by expected information gain rather than chosen randomly.
Active learning research studies strategies for selecting examples that are most useful for labeling or model improvement [15,16].
Moodify can use a conservative form of this idea: prioritize cases that are uncertain, representative of a cluster, high-consequence, or likely to resolve a known boundary.
The purpose is not to create an endlessly self-optimizing system.
It is to make limited human review produce the greatest improvement in the Ear's knowledge boundary.
A track-level confidence can hide local uncertainty.
Ear v1 should preserve confidence trajectories where judgments depend on local evidence.
A report can show that a finding is strongly supported from 47-52 seconds but ambiguous elsewhere.
This is more precise than assigning one confidence to the entire track.
Temporal uncertainty also helps debug structural transitions and generator artifacts that appear intermittently.
Repeated sections provide another axis for uncertainty.
If a phenomenon appears consistently across three choruses, confidence in it being structurally intentional may rise.
If it appears in only one repetition, anomaly confidence may rise.
The important point is that repetition changes belief without changing the underlying physical observation.
Nearest-neighbor retrieval can look persuasive even when all neighbors are far away.
Moodify should therefore report both rank and absolute distance/density.
A top match is not meaningful if the query lies outside the validated corpus.
Retrieval confidence should depend on whether the neighborhood itself is credible.
This is essential when using the case library as evidence for new generator families.
Calibration is not a permanent property of a model.
It depends on the model, data distribution, prevalence, judgment definition and sometimes deployment policy.
A calibration identity can be represented as: Historical judgments should retain the calibration model they actually used.
A new calibration should create a new judgment version or rerendering context, not rewrite the old confidence silently.
Natural-language explanations can unintentionally erase uncertainty.
Phrases such as “this is caused by” or “the track has” sound categorical even when the machine's internal state is probabilistic.

Moodify should map uncertainty state to language policy. | Internal state | Preferred language | | --- | --- | | high calibrated support | “Moodify detects…” / “Evidence supports…” | | moderate support | “Likely…” / “The pattern is consistent with…” | | low support | “Possible…” / “One hypothesis is…” | | uncertain | “The evidence is inconclusive…” | | insufficient evidence | “Moodify cannot determine this from the available evidence.” | | unknown anomaly | “An unusual pattern is present, but it does not match a validated class.” | Language should never be more certain than the JudgmentRecord.

A report generator is not authorized to upgrade “possible” into “definite.” This is particularly important for AI-artifact attribution, where causal evidence may be weak even if pattern similarity is high.

The first production policy can remain simple but explicit. | Condition | Ear v1 semantic output | | --- | --- | | required evidence missing | INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE | | evidence complete but calibrated support below family threshold | UNCERTAIN | | OOD/novelty high | reduce confidence; forbid strong causal wording | | sensor disagreement high | surface conflict; reduce authority | | high severity + uncertain | human review candidate | | novel recurring cluster | UNKNOWN_ANOMALY_CANDIDATE / research queue | | supported + calibrated + evidence complete | authoritative judgment | The thresholds are not fixed by this chapter.
They must be estimated per family from validation cases.
The architecture requirement is that such thresholds exist, are versioned and can be audited.
The policy should be conservative for causal or novel artifact labels and more permissive for direct physical findings with strong measurement support.
It should evaluate whether confidence changes in the expected direction.
A mature Ear should be rewarded when it becomes more certain for the right reasons and less certain for the right reasons.
The Intervention Lab can create uncertainty tests as well as detection tests.
Examples include gradually reducing signal-to-noise ratio, partially masking a transient, weakening a phase manipulation, corrupting one sensor's input, or introducing a novel codec chain.
As evidence weakens, confidence should generally fall before the judgment flips unpredictably.
This provides a calibration-like physical test: the Ear's certainty should respond smoothly to controlled degradation of evidence where the phenomenon permits it.
A database that also records where the Ear was uncertain is more valuable because it maps the frontier of the system's knowledge.

Over time, Moodify can identify recurring uncertainty clusters: generator families the Ear does not understand, structural contexts that confuse phase judgments, artifact signatures lacking labels, or confidence ranges with poor calibration.
The unknowns are no longer invisible failures; they become prioritized assets for the next Ear version.
The uncertainty corpus is therefore part of Moodify's technical memory.
Uncertainty as Intelligence can be summarized by twelve principles. **1.
Confidence is earned empirically.** Model scores are not probabilities by default. **2.
Uncertainty has causes.** Signal ambiguity, model ignorance, missing evidence and distribution shift are different. **3.
Local uncertainty is preserved.** Final confidence does not erase where uncertainty originated. **4.
Calibration is versioned.** Reliability changes when models and distributions change. **5.
OOD is evidence, not diagnosis.** Novel does not mean defective. **6.
Disagreement is informative.** Conflicting sensors or models remain visible. **7.
Dependency matters.** Correlated evidence cannot be counted as independent certainty. **8.
Abstention is a decision.** The Ear can refuse semantic overreach. **9.
Coverage and risk are co-measured.** Reliability cannot be optimized by hiding all hard cases. **10.
Unknowns become research states.** Novel cases can seed new knowledge. **11.
Human attention follows information value and consequence.** **12.
Moodify Ear becomes more intelligent when it becomes less willing to pretend.
Uncertainty is the mechanism that allows the system to preserve the boundary between evidence and assertion.

A trustworthy Ear can be certain when physical and contextual evidence align, cautious when hypotheses compete, silent when required evidence is absent, and curious when a case lies outside its known world.
Unknown and uncertain cases stop disappearing into generic error metrics.
They become a structured map of what the Ear has not yet learned.
The question “Can machines learn to hear?” therefore contains another question inside it: *Can a machine learn what it does not yet know?* Moodify Ear v1 must begin to answer yes.

claim: These principles map naturally onto Moodify's evidence, explanation, faithfulness and uncertainty layers.

Moodify can represent supporting relations as a directed graph: Nodes may represent source audio, time ranges, sensor outputs, representation fields, structural entities, retrieved cases, model scores, hypotheses, judgments and rendered artifacts.
Edges represent relations such as DERIVED_FROM, SUPPORTS, CONTRADICTS, ALIGNS_WITH, GENERATED_BY or RENDERED_AS.
W3C PROV provides a general vocabulary for representing entities, activities and agents in provenance records [2,3].
Moodify need not implement the full standard, but its evidence graph should preserve the same core idea: important data objects remain connected to the activities and versions that produced them.
A judgment can be explained at a high level, then progressively expanded until the reviewer reaches the underlying measurement.
Explanations that cannot identify where evidence occurs are often too weak for engineering review.

Every time-localized finding should include a support interval: The interval can be expressed in seconds and, where MSE is available, in musical coordinates such as bar, phrase, section or lyric line.

This turns a report from “the track has unstable stereo” into “47.2-52.1 s, chorus 2, bars 33-36, contains the strongest anti-correlated low-frequency evidence.” Time localization also allows reviewers to listen directly to the relevant region rather than search through the entire track.
A judgment may depend on evidence at several time-frequency scales.
A transient anomaly may need tens of milliseconds.
A spectral balance judgment may need seconds or sections.
Evidence should therefore record its resolution: The resolution used for explanation should match the phenomenon.
A whole-track average is poor evidence for a local glitch.
A 20 ms frame is poor evidence for a macro-dynamic judgment.
This principle mirrors the multi-resolution architecture of WSE and MSE.

A useful Ear v1 evidence object should contain more than a filename pointing to an image. | Field | Purpose | | --- | --- | | evidence_id | stable identity | | semantic_role | what claim this artifact supports | | source/case/run | hearing-event identity | | time/frequency support | where evidence applies | | content reference | data, plot, audio excerpt, table, score | | producer/version | sensor/model/render method | | parameters | window, transform, threshold, etc. | | content hash | integrity | | status/quality | valid, degraded, failed, provisional | The content hash protects integrity.
The producer and parameter set make the artifact reproducible.
The semantic role explains why it belongs in the case.
The support interval connects it to the sound.
Evidence without semantic role becomes archival clutter.
Evidence without provenance becomes unverifiable.
Evidence without localization becomes difficult to inspect.

A useful explanation can be modeled as an argument with premises, context, inference and conclusion.
Premises are measurements or validated structural facts.
Context identifies the reference and musical situation.
The inference specifies the rule, model or reasoning step.
A reviewer can challenge a premise, a reference, the inference or the conclusion rather than rejecting an opaque paragraph.
Moodify should therefore store explanation structure separately from its final natural-language rendering.
AI-generated music especially demands this discipline because many different generation, codec and post-production processes can create similar acoustic symptoms.
Moodify can be useful without pretending to know the entire causal chain.

section: 11. Faithfulness: Does the Explanation Reflect the Model?
claim: Moodify should therefore evaluate explanation faithfulness rather than relying on visual plausibility.
A straightforward faithfulness test removes or alters the evidence claimed to matter and measures the judgment response.
If a model claims that a narrow high-frequency region drives an artifact prediction, attenuating that region should reduce the score more than attenuating irrelevant regions, all else being equal.

Recent audio-XAI work has increasingly benchmarked explanations using controlled time- or frequency-localized perturbations, precisely because qualitative saliency maps alone do not establish faithfulness [5,6].
The Intervention Lab provides Moodify with a natural mechanism for such tests.

Audio has an advantage over many domains: part of an explanation can itself be listened to. audioLIME introduced listenable explanations by using source separation to create musically meaningful perturbations for local explanation [7].
Other work has explored audible or directly time-domain interpretations of audio classifiers [8,9].
A report may provide a short evidence excerpt, a mono fold-down comparison, a filtered comparison or a controlled residual where the comparison is semantically valid.
The explanation should remain faithful to the original case.
A transformed example must be labeled as a derived analytical artifact, not confused with the source.
An explanation can sound intuitively convincing yet fail to reflect the model's true decision path.
Conversely, a faithful explanation may be difficult for a human to interpret.
Moodify should therefore evaluate at least two axes: Human interpretability and model faithfulness are complementary objectives.
For deterministic engineering rules, faithfulness is usually easier because the evidence path is explicit.
For learned artifact models, post-hoc explanations require stronger validation.
Some judgment paths are interpretable by construction.
A clipping rule can directly expose samples, threshold and time locations.

Others rely on complex learned models and require post-hoc interpretation. | Type | Example | Strength | Risk | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | intrinsic | threshold/rule with explicit measurements | direct audit path | rule scope may be too broad | | post-hoc | saliency/attribution for learned classifier | can inspect opaque model | may be unfaithful or unstable | | example-based | retrieved validated cases | human-comparable | corpus/metric bias | | counterfactual | minimal evidence change flips finding | reveals boundary | may create unrealistic changes | Ear v1 should prefer intrinsically interpretable mechanisms for direct physical judgments when they are sufficient.
Learned models should be introduced where they add capability that simpler mechanisms cannot provide.
This is not an ideological preference for simple models.
It is an allocation of explanation burden: opaque models must earn their place by delivering additional hearing capability.
Feature-attribution methods estimate which input dimensions contribute to a model output.
Integrated Gradients, Grad-CAM, SHAP and LIME are widely used examples across machine learning [10-13].
For audio, the input dimensions may be waveform samples, spectrogram bins, time-frequency patches, source components or representation features.
Attribution should be interpreted as model sensitivity under a method's assumptions, not as a causal explanation of the physical world.
Moodify should record attribution-method identity and parameters just as it records sensor versions.
A colorful heatmap can appear meaningful even when it is weakly connected to the learned model.
Sanity-check research has shown that some saliency methods can remain visually similar after model parameters or labels are randomized [14].
Moodify should therefore avoid presenting saliency visualizations as evidence merely because they look intuitive.
At minimum, explanation methods used in production should pass model-randomization, label-randomization or perturbation-style checks appropriate to the model family.
Visual explanation is an instrument that must itself be validated.
A counterfactual asks: what minimal change would alter the judgment?
For a phase-risk finding, a counterfactual might ask how much inter-channel phase relation must change before the risk falls below the family threshold.
For a high-frequency-cutoff finding, it might ask what restoration of upper-band energy would eliminate the finding.
Counterfactuals are useful because they reveal the decision boundary, but they must not be confused with a recommendation to modify the music.
In Ear-only Phase I, they are analytical tools.
Counterfactual evidence can also test whether the Judgment Engine responds to physically relevant variables rather than shortcuts.
Humans often ask explanations in contrastive form: why this judgment rather than another?
Why was chorus 2 flagged but chorus 1 was not?
Why is this bandwidth change considered anomalous while another is considered structural?
Moodify can answer using paired representation differences: Contrastive explanations are particularly powerful when MSE provides repeated sections.
The system can show exactly which WSE dimensions differ between structurally equivalent regions.
This turns explanation into comparison rather than an isolated description.
Repeated musical structure creates natural internal controls.
If chorus 1 and chorus 3 share a stable spectral profile while chorus 2 exhibits a unique collapse above 16 kHz, the contrast itself becomes evidence.
The explanation can state that the finding is not merely absolute, but relative to structurally matched peers inside the same track.
This is often stronger than comparing the song with a broad genre population because it controls for instrumentation, production identity and artistic context.
The Production Case library allows case-based explanation.
A new finding can be supported by similarity to previously reviewed cases.
The explanation should expose which cases were retrieved, what representation view was used and how far away the neighbors were.
A statement such as “this region resembles 12 previously reviewed bandwidth-limitation cases” is useful only if the retrieval corpus and distance are known.
Case retrieval should supplement physical evidence rather than replace it when direct physical evidence exists.
Explanations should not contain only supporting evidence.
Absence of expected evidence or evidence against a hypothesis can be equally important.
For hypothesis h: For example, a codec-artifact hypothesis may be weakened if the expected bandwidth boundary is absent.
A phase-risk hypothesis may be weakened if mono fold-down remains stable despite a low broadband correlation.
Representing contradictory evidence makes the Ear less likely to tell one-sided stories.
A judgment can be correct but inadequately evidenced.
Moodify should therefore measure evidence completeness separately from prediction correctness.
Mandatory evidence depends on judgment family.
A complete clipping finding may require fewer artifacts than a causal artifact attribution.
A finding with missing mandatory evidence should be downgraded, abstained or blocked from authoritative reporting according to policy.
This converts explainability into a testable production gate.

section: 24. Explanation Accuracy Is Not Prediction Accuracy
claim: The strongest Ear v1 case is one in which the judgment is correct, the explanation faithfully reflects the decision, and the evidence corresponds to a meaningful acoustic phenomenon.
Small irrelevant changes to the input should not radically alter the explanation.
If metadata changes, the acoustic evidence should remain stable.
If a lossless file is rewrapped, a spectrogram-based explanation should not move dramatically.
Stability should not be demanded under genuinely relevant acoustic change.
The purpose is to test robustness to transformations that should preserve the semantics of the case.
Explanation instability can reveal fragile attribution methods even when predictions remain stable.
An explanation method can fail when the model is outside its familiar domain.
A saliency map may still look precise even when the underlying classifier is uncertain.
Moodify should therefore propagate OOD and uncertainty state into explanation language and presentation.
A low-confidence or out-of-distribution finding can still expose evidence, but the explanation should clearly state that interpretation is provisional.
Precision of visualization must never be mistaken for precision of knowledge.
An explanation is useful only if the intended reviewer can understand it.

The same case may need several views. | Audience | Preferred projection | | --- | --- | | creator/listener | plain finding, location, concise reason, audible excerpt | | audio engineer | measurements, curves, time-frequency evidence, thresholds | | researcher | representation fields, attribution diagnostics, retrieved cases | | auditor | provenance, versions, hashes, state/evidence completeness | | model developer | raw scores, calibration, attribution/perturbation results | The technical evidence remains the same, but the projection changes.
Engineers may need phase curves and transform parameters.
Creators may need a time-local statement and an audible excerpt.
Researchers may need representation vectors and model diagnostics.
The machine-readable evidence graph should remain authoritative across all views.
Meaningful explanation is therefore a presentation problem built on top of a stable evidence problem.
Moodify should avoid flooding the user with every measurement.
The report can reveal evidence progressively.

A three-level pattern is useful: | Level | Content | | --- | --- | | 1 - finding | one-sentence judgment + severity/confidence + location | | 2 - evidence summary | key measurements, reference, structural context | | 3 - audit view | full artifacts, provenance, model/rule versions, explanation tests | Progressive disclosure preserves technical depth without turning the primary report into a laboratory console.
The important architectural rule is that deeper levels are available because the evidence was preserved at run time.
For each authoritative finding, Moodify can package a compact Auditory Evidence Bundle.
The bundle is the smallest portable object that allows another reviewer or future Ear version to inspect the finding without reopening the entire internal runtime.
It can be embedded in the Production Case package and referenced by the Auditory Report.
Evidence artifacts should use stable identity rather than human-only filenames.
A canonical ID can be derived from: Human-readable names remain useful, but the content hash and semantic metadata prevent accidental substitution.
If a plot is regenerated under a new rendering style but from identical canonical data, Moodify should be able to distinguish the visual derivative from the underlying evidence dataset.
The Production Case is where evidence becomes durable.
Every final judgment should point to an Evidence Bundle, and every bundle should resolve to artifacts inside or referenced by the case.
Human review can then annotate not only whether the judgment was correct, but whether the explanation was useful, faithful and complete.
These review outcomes become LearningRecords for both the hearing model and the explanation system.

Explanation errors should be classified separately from judgment errors. | Explanation review outcome | Likely change target | | --- | --- | | evidence incorrect | sensor/evidence extraction | | evidence incomplete | judgment-family evidence contract | | explanation unfaithful | XAI method / model interface | | language overstates certainty | rendering policy | | causal overreach | epistemic-level policy | | too technical / not meaningful | audience projection | | unstable under irrelevant change | explanation method / model robustness | | artifact/provenance missing | PPE packaging | A correct judgment with an unfaithful explanation is still a defect.
A correct explanation with missing provenance is still incomplete.
A technically accurate explanation that no intended reviewer can understand may require a presentation change rather than a model change.
The taxonomy keeps explainability engineering targeted.
Ear v1 does not need a universal explanation engine.
Learned artifact hypotheses can use more experimental XAI methods, but their authority should remain lower until faithfulness is demonstrated.
This ordering allows Moodify to build trust from the inside out.
Moodify can adapt this principle to its own judgment families: explanations should identify the regions and features that truly alter the decision.
Benchmarking explanation turns “trust me” into an engineering test.

section: 35. The Difference Between Evidence and Persuasion
claim: A trustworthy Ear should be easier to disagree with, because its premises are visible.
Without evidence, a past judgment is a historical opinion.
With evidence, a future researcher can re-evaluate it under a new theory.
This is especially important because Moodify Ear is expected to evolve.
A case that Ear v1 labeled as UNKNOWN_ANOMALY may become explainable under Ear v3.
If the original WSE/MSE evidence and provenance were preserved, the new model can reinterpret history without inventing it.
The evidence corpus therefore becomes a second-order asset: not only data about sound, but data about why the system believed what it believed.
Such a corpus can support benchmark construction, model debugging, rule refinement, explanation research and institutional memory.
Evidence and Explainable Hearing can be summarized by twelve principles. **1.
Judgment without evidence is assertion.** **2.
Evidence, explanation and provenance are distinct but linked.** **3.
Explanation must be grounded in the auditory record.** **4.
Evidence resolution must match the phenomenon.** **6.
Explanation is a structured argument, not a paragraph.** **7.
Human interpretability does not guarantee model faithfulness.** **9.
Causal language requires causal evidence.** **10.
Contradictory evidence remains visible.** **11.
Explanation quality is independently reviewable and benchmarkable.** **12.
The Ear must always be able to move backward from a claim to the sound.**
Moodify Ear has now acquired not only a way to judge, but a way to justify.
Evidence binds semantic claims to physical and structural observations.
Provenance binds those observations to the system that produced them.
Explanation organizes the chain into a form that a human can inspect.
The strongest explanation is not the longest one.
It is the one that exposes exactly the evidence needed, at the right resolution, with the correct uncertainty, while preserving a path back to the source.
The Ear is no longer a black box that returns conclusions.
It becomes a system whose claims can be tested, contradicted, reviewed and inherited.
Explainable hearing is therefore not a layer of communication added after intelligence.
It is one of the mechanisms by which auditory intelligence becomes trustworthy knowledge.

The Auditory Report can be summarized by twelve principles. **1.
Report is projection, not truth source.** **2.
Machine record and human view are separate but linked.** **3.
Location, reference, severity, confidence and evidence remain visible.** **5.
A universal quality score is avoided until validated for a specific purpose.** **6.
Uncertainty receives dedicated report space.** **7.
Historical reports can be regenerated without re-hearing.** **11.
Different audiences receive different views of the same case.** **12.
The report is the principal human interface to review and learning.**
The Auditory Report is where Moodify Ear becomes legible.
Uncertainty defines the boundary of confidence.
The report organizes all of these into a human artifact.
Its job is not to make Moodify appear intelligent.
Its job is to expose the intelligence that actually exists, including its limits.
A good Auditory Report lets a user understand what the Ear heard, where it heard it, why it matters, how sure the system is, what evidence supports the claim, and what remains unknown.
That report is not the end of the hearing process.
It is the interface through which machine hearing becomes reviewable knowledge.

**Technical Monographs - Volume I** **Chapter XIII - The Production Case** **August 2026** > A run ends.
A software task begins when a command is invoked and ends when computation stops.
It remains meaningful after the execution has ended because the conditions, evidence, judgment, review and lineage of the event are preserved.
If a song is analyzed today and the result cannot be reconstructed six months later, the organization has retained an output but lost the hearing event.
If the result can be linked to its source, representation, judgment, evidence, uncertainty and review, the event can become knowledge.

The Production Case is the smallest durable unit in which Moodify can say: *this is what the Ear heard, this is how it heard it, this is what it concluded, this is what the evidence showed, and this is what later review changed.* This chapter defines the Production Case as the institutional memory of Moodify Ear.

A completed case can later show exactly which capabilities were required and which were optional.
If a case requests a judgment family whose required sensor is unavailable, the system can fail or degrade before expensive execution begins.
The Production Case passes through explicit states.
The state identifies which claims are currently authorized.
A case with measurements but no validated judgments is not equivalent to a completed case.
A case with judgments but unresolved mandatory evidence is not ready for authoritative packaging.
The state machine therefore protects semantic meaning, not merely orchestration.
Ear v1 may use a detailed lifecycle with source registration, specification, analysis, technical validation, approval boundaries where required, execution, verification, packaging and completion.
The exact labels may evolve, but invalid semantic shortcuts should remain impossible.
A robust lifecycle is easier to audit when transitions are recorded as events rather than only updating one mutable status field.
Each transition event records prior state, next state, timestamp, actor/subsystem, reason and relevant version context.
The current state can be derived from the event history.
This creates a chronological case narrative and makes recovery safer because the system knows what has already happened.
Event sourcing is a broader software pattern for deriving system state from an immutable sequence of facts [1].
Moodify need not adopt a full event-sourced architecture, but the principle is valuable for case traceability.
A Production Case can generate many artifacts.

They should be indexed by role rather than scattered across directories. | Artifact class | Examples | | --- | --- | | identity/spec | source record, case spec, config/version manifest | | measurement | WSE/MSE sensor outputs | | representation | Auditory Representation v1 arrays/records | | judgment | JudgmentRecords and uncertainty state | | evidence | Evidence Bundles, plots, excerpts, comparisons | | report | machine JSON, PDF/app render | | review | HumanReview records | | learning | LearningRecords/candidate links | | operations | logs, validation, packaging manifest | Every artifact should identify its producer, content hash, semantic role, source/run relationship and version.
The index can distinguish canonical artifacts from optional research artifacts.
The case remains understandable even when storage locations change because logical identities are separated from physical paths.

Moodify should distinguish canonical records from derived views. | Canonical | Derived | | --- | --- | | source identity record | decoded preview / thumbnail | | measurement/representation records | visual plots | | JudgmentRecord | finding card / report sentence | | Evidence Bundle metadata | rendered evidence figure | | HumanReview | review summary UI | | LearningRecord | project-management task derived from it | A JudgmentRecord is canonical.
A PDF page that renders the judgment is derived.
A canonical measurement array may generate several visualizations.
If a derived artifact is lost, it can often be regenerated.
If a canonical record is lost, the historical hearing may become irrecoverable.
Retention and backup policy should reflect this hierarchy.
The MeasurementRecord binds the sensor outputs to a specific run and source.
It should include sensor status as well as values.
Failed, not-run and insufficient-quality outputs remain distinguishable.
The MeasurementRecord is the first durable layer above raw audio.
It allows later representation or judgment experiments without re-decoding the source when the preserved measurements are sufficient.
The case stores the versioned Auditory Representation that the Judgment Engine consumed.
This is critical for historical reproducibility.
If Representation v2 later changes field semantics, Ear v1 judgments remain tied to Representation v1.
A later re-analysis may create a derived representation, but it should not overwrite the original case state.
The Production Case thus becomes the place where representation history remains concrete rather than theoretical.
A case may contain multiple JudgmentRecords, each with its own identity and evidence requirements.
The set should include supported, uncertain, insufficient-evidence and unknown-anomaly outcomes where relevant.
The absence of a positive finding is not equivalent to proof of normality unless the judgment family executed with sufficient coverage.
This is why case-level capability coverage must be stored alongside judgment output.
Every authoritative finding should resolve to one or more Auditory Evidence Bundles.
The case therefore preserves not only the conclusion but the argument that supported it.
If a future researcher disagrees with the judgment, the original evidence remains available.
Evidence bundles also support selective invalidation.

An Ear can analyze one thousand songs without learning anything.
If every case ends as a report and disappears from the future behavior of the system, the software has processed data but has not accumulated intelligence.
Learning begins when experience changes the system in a controlled and measurable way.
For Moodify, that experience is not raw audio alone.
It is the combination of source, measurements, representation, judgment, uncertainty, evidence and human review preserved inside validated Production Cases.

The question “Can an Ear learn?” therefore becomes operational: *can reviewed hearing events produce better future hearing without destroying what was already known?* This chapter defines the answer as a case-based, versioned and gated learning loop rather than continuous silent adaptation.
The core learning loop is: Each arrow has a different meaning.
HumanReview does not directly change a model.
LearningRecord does not automatically become production policy.
CandidateUpdate does not become authority until it passes validation.
Promotion creates a new version whose behavior can be compared with the previous one.
This separation is what allows the Ear to learn while remaining historically reproducible.
A confidence error may require recalibration without changing the underlying class model.
A novel artifact cluster may require a new representation field before any classifier is trained.
The LearningRecord should therefore identify the target layer explicitly.
Learning becomes more efficient when the system knows *what kind of mistake it made*.

Regression protection is what separates learning from patching.
Continual learning introduces a classic danger: a model that learns new information may lose performance on previously learned tasks.
This phenomenon is commonly called catastrophic forgetting [3,4].
For Moodify, forgetting could appear when a new artifact detector improves on a recent generator family but begins misclassifying older validated material.
Ear learning must therefore be evaluated across historical benchmark slices, not only on new cases.
The simplest defense in Ear v1 is not sophisticated continual-learning algorithms.

Moodify Ear cannot be validated only by asking whether its reports sound plausible.

If the system claims to detect a high-frequency cutoff, phase instability or transient damage, the strongest early test is to create the phenomenon deliberately and ask whether the Ear responds to the known change.
The Intervention Lab is therefore not a post-processing product.
It is a scientific side loop attached to the Ear.
Its purpose is to generate controlled derivatives of known source audio so that measurement, representation, judgment, uncertainty and evidence can be tested against a declared physical intervention.
The central idea is simple: if the experimenter knows exactly what changed, the Ear can be evaluated against stronger ground truth than ordinary finished music usually provides.
The governing principle is: *the Lab changes the sound; the product listens.*

An intervention is a transformation T with parameter alpha applied to source x: The parameter alpha controls intervention strength: cutoff frequency, compression ratio, clipping threshold, channel delay, noise level, codec bitrate or another physically defined quantity.
Because T and alpha are known, the experiment contains causal information.
Moodify can test whether the corresponding WSE field moves in the expected direction and whether the Judgment Engine responds at appropriate strengths.
This does not prove that the same pattern in a natural song was caused by T.
It proves that the Ear can hear the acoustic consequences produced by T.
Every experiment should be a special Production Case family rather than an ad hoc script.
The parent source, transformation identity, parameter vector, derivative source hash, expected physical effect and blind Ear result remain linked.
The intervention metadata is hidden from the hearing path until evaluation.

This creates reproducible experiments that can later enter benchmarks, regression tests and learning datasets without losing provenance. | Field | Purpose | | --- | --- | | ParentSourceID | identity of untouched reference source | | TransformID/version | exact intervention implementation | | parameter vector | strength and settings | | DerivedSourceID | content identity of transformed audio | | expected physical effect | declared before Ear evaluation | | blind Ear CaseID | ordinary canonical analysis of derivative | | control group | positive/negative/sham relation | | evaluation | sensor/judgment/localization/uncertainty results |
If the Ear receives the intervention type as metadata, the experiment becomes meaningless.
The derivative should enter the canonical hearing pipeline as ordinary audio, with only normal source metadata available.
The evaluator may know the expected effect; the Ear should not.
This is analogous to blinding in experimental design: information that could bias the measurement process is withheld from the system being evaluated.
For machine pipelines, leakage can occur through filenames, directories, tags, sidecar JSON, codec names or intervention-specific sample rates.
The Lab should randomize or normalize such cues where they are not part of the tested phenomenon.
This is also a defense against shortcut learning.

claim: Controls transform the question from “did the model flag this one file?” to “does the Ear respond specifically to the intended acoustic variable?”
A single before/after pair is less informative than a controlled strength series.
For parameter levels alpha_0 < alpha_1 < ... < alpha_n, Moodify can analyze a family of derivatives.
Physical features should change in a predictable direction where the intervention is monotonic.
Judgment confidence may remain low at subtle levels and then rise as evidence becomes clearer.
This allows the team to estimate detection thresholds, sensitivity zones, saturation and instability near decision boundaries.
Intervention experiments support direct definitions of sensitivity and specificity for a judgment family.
Sensitivity asks whether the Ear responds when the relevant phenomenon is deliberately present.
Specificity asks whether it remains quiet under irrelevant or nuisance transformations.
A detector that fires on every transformed file has high apparent sensitivity and no useful specificity.
Borrowing the language of experimental science, intervention strength can be treated as a dose and the Ear response as a response variable.
Some phenomena become perceptually or technically relevant only after a threshold.
Others should show gradual physical change even if the semantic judgment remains unchanged until policy criteria are crossed.
Dose-response analysis is especially useful for separating sensor quality from judgment policy.
A sensor may track the intervention smoothly while the Judgment Engine changes category only once.
A controlled low-pass or high-shelf attenuation is one of the cleanest WSE experiments.
The Lab can vary cutoff frequency, slope and attenuation depth while preserving other properties as much as practical.
Expected evidence includes reduced high-band energy, a lower bandwidth estimate, altered spectral tilt and a persistent frequency boundary where the transformation is strong.
The Ear should not automatically label every low-pass derivative an AI artifact.
The validated claim is that bandwidth limitation is detected.
A sham export with identical audio samples but changed container metadata should not trigger the bandwidth finding.
A low-shelf boost or narrow-band resonance can create controlled low-frequency accumulation.
Expected WSE responses include increased low-band energy, altered low/mid ratio, changed crest behavior and possibly stereo/phase effects if the intervention is channel-specific.
MSE can be used to test context sensitivity: the same low-frequency change applied only to one chorus should be compared with matched chorus repetitions.
This experiment therefore validates both physical detection and structure-conditioned interpretation.
Compression experiments can vary threshold, ratio, attack, release and makeup gain.
Makeup gain should be controlled carefully because loudness change can confound dynamic change.
Expected observations include reduced crest factor, altered short-term loudness variation, changed transient shape and reduced macro- or micro-dynamic contrast depending on parameters.
An important experimental design is loudness-matched comparison.
If compressed and reference derivatives are matched in integrated loudness, the Ear must rely more directly on dynamic evidence rather than simple level differences.
Limiting and clipping should be tested separately.
A limiter can reduce peaks with relatively smooth nonlinear behavior; hard clipping truncates waveform amplitude above a threshold.
Hard clipping provides especially clear ground truth because clipped sample regions and thresholds can be calculated exactly.
The Ear should localize them and distinguish the condition from true-peak risk that occurs without stored-sample clipping.
Parametric clipping series are useful Golden Cases because their expected sample-domain behavior is deterministic.
Transient interventions can soften attacks through limiting, envelope shaping, low-pass filtering of attacks or controlled convolution.
The goal is to create known changes in onset sharpness without broadly altering the rest of the signal.
Expected responses can include lower positive spectral flux, slower local attack slopes and reduced peak-to-local-energy ratios.
Because transient perception is context-dependent, the Lab should test percussion-dominant, vocal, plucked and sustained material separately rather than assuming one threshold across all sources.
A simple gain offset between left and right channels creates a controlled stereo-level imbalance.
The intervention can be static or time-varying.
Expected evidence includes L/R energy difference and corresponding changes in M/S representation.
A nuisance control can apply equal gain to both channels.
The overall loudness changes, but the stereo-imbalance judgment should remain stable.
Inter-channel delay and polarity manipulation create controlled changes in phase and mono compatibility.
Small sample delays can create frequency-dependent phase differences; polarity inversion creates a more extreme anti-correlated condition when channels are otherwise similar.
Expected evidence includes changes in local correlation, inter-channel phase relations, M/S energy and mono fold-down cancellation.
The Ear should distinguish unusual phase from demonstrated mono-loss risk by using the actual fold-down evidence.
Noise can test robustness and evidence degradation.
White, pink, band-limited or shaped noise may be added at controlled signal-to-noise ratios.
First, they test direct artifact/noise sensors.
Second, they provide an uncertainty experiment: as SNR decreases, confidence in unrelated tasks such as pitch, structure or transient detection should degrade appropriately.
A trustworthy Ear should become less certain before becoming nonsensical.
Lossy codecs can introduce bandwidth restriction, pre-echo, temporal smearing and quantization-like artifacts depending on codec, bitrate and signal content.
Codec experiments should record encoder identity, version, profile, bitrate mode, sample rate and all relevant parameters.
A decoded PCM derivative should be hashed and analyzed as the Ear input.
Reference-based residual analysis is valid here because the original and coded-decoded derivative are explicitly paired.

Perceptual audio-quality standards such as ITU-R BS.1387 provide historical context for reference-based perceptual evaluation, while Moodify uses the pair primarily to validate its own evidence pathways [1].
The Ear may confidently detect bandwidth restriction without being able to determine whether the cause was a codec, generator, export setting or deliberate filter.
The Lab is useful because a codec intervention supplies known cause.
This difference should appear in the ontology: *detectable physical consequence* is a stronger claim than *causal attribution*.
Intervention Cases teach the Ear which acoustic consequences are compatible with particular causes, but do not make cause uniquely identifiable in the wild.
Broad equalization changes can test spectral-balance measurements and population-reference policies.
The Lab can apply low shelf, high shelf, broad bell filters or smooth tilt transformations.
These experiments should distinguish sensor validation from aesthetic judgment.
The sensor should recover the known spectral change.
Whether the change is a problem depends on structural and reference context.
This makes equalization experiments useful for testing that WSE remains descriptive while the Judgment Engine remains conditional.
Narrow boosts or notches can create controlled resonances and spectral holes.
These are useful for testing frequency resolution and local evidence localization.
Different STFT or filterbank resolutions should be compared to determine which sensor scale resolves the phenomenon reliably.
The result can inform the multi-resolution sensor design rather than only the judgment threshold.
Clicks, dropouts, micro-silences, duplicated frames or abrupt splice boundaries can test waveform morphology and transient anomaly detection.
Because the intervention time is exact, localization error can be measured directly.
This supports an important metric beyond classification: how accurately does the Ear identify *where* the event occurred?
Temporal interventions can also test report localization and evidence excerpt generation end to end.
Some experiments should affect only one channel or one derived source role.
This tests whether Moodify preserves channel/source provenance instead of collapsing everything into whole-track summaries.
Examples include left-only high-frequency loss, right-only clipping, low-band polarity inversion or transient softening applied to a separated drum estimate.
When estimated stems are used, the separator version and artifacts must be recorded because the intervention is now conditional on an estimated source rather than a studio stem.
MSE enables interventions applied to musically meaningful regions: one chorus, one phrase, one bar or one lyric line.
These experiments test whether the Ear can use repeated musical structure as an internal control.
If chorus 2 alone receives a spectral cutoff, the report should be able to say that chorus 2 differs from chorus 1 and chorus 3.
This validates the integration of WSE, MSE, Judgment and Evidence rather than only one sensor.
Real audio problems can combine multiple phenomena.
Factorial experiments vary two or more interventions systematically.
For example, compression and high-frequency attenuation can be varied independently to test whether one finding masks or exaggerates the other.
Stereo imbalance and phase delay can be combined to test evidence disentanglement.
Factorial designs reveal interactions, but their combinatorial cost grows quickly.
Ear v1 should use small targeted designs after single-factor behavior is stable.
An intervention often changes more than one measurable quantity.
Compression changes level distribution and transients.
A codec changes spectrum and time-domain behavior.
A filter can alter phase depending on implementation.
The purpose is not perfect laboratory purity.
Experiment order, derivative filenames and run order should be randomized where operationally practical.
This reduces accidental correlations between intervention identity and runtime artifacts.
Randomization is especially useful when GPU/CPU load, caching or time-dependent environment conditions could influence learned components.
The randomization seed belongs in the Intervention Case manifest so the study can be reproduced.
A single source can produce misleading conclusions.
Intervention experiments should be replicated across diverse source material.
For each intervention family, the benchmark should include several production styles, dynamic ranges, spectral profiles and structural contexts.
The response should be evaluated across sources rather than only on one convenient test song.
Replication distinguishes a detector of the physical phenomenon from a detector of one source-specific side effect.
Intervention sources should be chosen deliberately.
Clean, diverse and rights-cleared material is preferable for long-term benchmark assets.
A balanced set may include vocal-led music, dense electronic material, acoustic/percussive music, bass-heavy mixes, sparse arrangements and already-limited masters.
Sources should also include challenging negatives: naturally dark mixes, intentionally wide mixes and dynamically dense styles.
These help prevent intervention-trained rules from becoming aesthetic dogma.

Every experiment should distinguish the expected physical effect from the expected semantic judgment. | Level | Example | | --- | --- | | known transformation | low-pass at 14 kHz | | expected physical effect | upper-band energy falls above cutoff | | expected WSE response | bandwidth estimate and high-band trajectory change | | possible interpretation | bandwidth limitation | | semantic judgment | depends on reference/context | | causal claim | known only inside intervention case; not necessarily inferable in wild case | A low-pass transformation guarantees spectral attenuation according to its filter response.
It does not guarantee that the final judgment should be “problem.” If applied intentionally to a bridge, the correct judgment may be ARTISTIC_CHARACTERISTIC or INFORMATIONAL.
This distinction prevents the Intervention Lab from teaching the Ear that every transformation is undesirable.
For each judgment family, a controlled series can estimate the intervention strength at which reliable detection begins.
The threshold should be reported with source variability and confidence rather than as one universal constant.
Different musical contexts can change observability.
Detection thresholds are properties of the Ear version and benchmark, not laws of human perception.
When the intervention has known onset and offset, the Ear can be evaluated on temporal localization.
This matters because an Ear that identifies the right phenomenon but points to the wrong part of the song is less useful for evidence and review.
Frequency-local interventions can similarly measure estimated-band error.
For a monotonic intervention, the sensor or evidence score should generally move in a consistent direction as strength increases.
Occasional non-monotonic behavior may be physically valid because of masking or nonlinear interactions, but systematic reversals are a warning that the feature or model is unstable.
Monotonicity tests are especially valuable for calibrating confidence and selecting operating ranges.
Intervention validation must also test what the Ear should ignore.
Changing filename, metadata, container wrapper, report language or lossless packaging should not change physical judgments.
Small gain changes should not alter phase judgments if the relevant inter-channel relation is preserved.
These tests expose shortcut features and hidden pipeline coupling.
The Lab can produce explicit counterfactuals: remove the suspected evidence and see whether the judgment disappears.
This is particularly useful for learned artifact models.
If a model claims to rely on a high-frequency pattern, modifying unrelated low-frequency energy should not have the same effect as repairing the high-frequency region.
Counterfactual tests link the Intervention Lab directly to explainability faithfulness from Chapter XI.
Intervention Cases can contribute to confidence calibration because the presence and strength of the physical phenomenon are known.
However, synthetic cases may be cleaner than naturally occurring cases.
Calibration should therefore combine controlled and natural reviewed cases rather than relying on the Lab alone.
The Lab is strongest for sensor sensitivity, threshold exploration and mechanism validation; natural Production Cases remain necessary for real-world prevalence and ambiguity.
A well-designed, reproducible Intervention Case can become a Golden Case.
The Golden version freezes source identity, transform implementation, parameters, expected physical response, Ear version contract and tolerances.
Future Ear releases can rerun these cases to ensure that known physical hearing has not regressed.
An intervention failure should create a LearningRecord just like a natural-case review.
If the Ear misses a known low-pass transformation, the target may be the WSE sensor.
If it measures the cutoff but fails to judge it, the target is the Judgment Engine.
If it judges correctly but explains the wrong band, the target is Evidence/Explainability.
The controlled nature of the experiment makes failure localization unusually strong.

The Lab should maintain a registry of approved intervention families and implementations. | Registry field | Example | | --- | --- | | family | HF_ATTENUATION | | transform version | lab.lowpass.v1.1 | | implementation | library/filter design/resampling policy | | parameter schema | cutoff, slope/order, attenuation | | primary expected effect | persistent high-band attenuation | | known secondary effects | phase/ringing depending implementation | | allowed source types | stereo PCM, specified sample rates | | benchmark status | research / validated / golden | Changing a filter library, codec implementation or resampling method can change the physical derivative.
Therefore intervention implementation versions are part of the benchmark contract.
A registry also prevents multiple researchers from using similarly named but technically different transformations.
An Intervention Case should be reconstructable from the original source and intervention specification wherever licensing permits.
Reproducibility requires transform version, parameter vector, numerical precision, random seed for stochastic interventions and environment dependencies.
The derivative audio itself should also be hashed, so reconstruction can be verified rather than assumed.
Eight to twelve deeply validated experiment families are more valuable than a large collection of uncalibrated effects.
The first matrix should align with the Ear v1 judgment families so every production claim has at least one controlled validation route where physically possible.
A detector may pass physical detection while causal attribution remains research-only.
The metric suite should make this distinction visible.
